If unflavored creatine leaves you bored—or worse, skipping your daily dose—Optimum Nutrition’s blueberry lemonade flavor might be the refresh your routine needs. Flavored creatine can make consistency easier, especially if you’re mixing it with water or combining it with other lightly flavored supplements.

When I tested it, I shook a serving into 10 ounces of cold water. A light foam formed at the top, but it didn’t interfere with the drinking experience. The powder dissolved smoothly, with no grit or residue.In terms of flavor, 10 ounces of water made it a little too light for my taste, but dialing it back to six to eight ounces gave it a bolder, slightly sweeter profile. It’s easy to drink on its own and flexible enough to mix with other supplements, though you’ll want to be mindful of potential flavor clashes.One thing to note: there’s no scoop included. You’ll need to measure it yourself with a teaspoon, but this is an intentional move by the brand to reduce plastic waste—a small, thoughtful gesture I appreciated.Each serving provides five grams of micronized creatine monohydrate and is Informed Choice-certified. Just note that it contains artificial flavors and sucralose.

To be clear, most creatine powders are technically vegan since creatine is synthetically made without animal by-products, according to a 2020 systematic review by the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Momentous Creatine offers third-party testing that goes beyond industry standards.

In my own testing, it blended smoothly in a shaker bottle with no taste or aftertaste, and only had minimal settling at the bottom. It wasn’t bothersome enough to take away from the experience, and the product’s quality more than makes up for any minor mixability quirks. Plus, the scoop has a long handle for easy grabbing without getting powder all over your hands. For those who want to avoid powder altogether, Momentous offers the same creatine formula in the form of creatine chews, available in three different flavors. At the core of the formula is Signature Spec creatine, a premium, patented form of micronized creatine monohydrate known for its consistency and high manufacturing standards. That means no fillers, hidden additives, and questionable extras—just reliable performance support in every scoop. Like the best overall, each serving delivers the clinically backed five-gram dose, confirmed through lab-verified testing. It’s also NSF Certified for Sport.

If you’re over large tubs crowding your pantry, Onnit Creatine proves that not every supplement needs to come in a bulky container. Whether you’re working with limited space or just prefer a cleaner, more minimalist setup, the smaller tub easily slides into a cabinet, gym bag, or drawer.

Inside, you get exactly what you want: five grams of creatine monohydrate per serving without fillers, sweeteners, or artificialflavors. It’s unflavored, ultra-simple, and Informed Sport-certified.The compact size means the powder sits closer to the lid, so scooping can get a little messy if you’re not careful. However, I felt like the smaller container was worth the minor inconvenience. In practice, the fine powder mixes smoothly into water or shakes, leaving just a slight trace of grit at the bottom—not enough to be distracting. Its neutral flavor also means it plays well with other supplements or blends seamlessly into smoothies without changing the taste.For anyone who values trusted testing and a no-nonsense package, Onnit Creatine is proof that great things can come in small containers.

If you travel often, mix your supplements on the go, or just don’t want to dig around for a scoop every day, Promix Non-GMO Creatine single-serve packets make things refreshingly simple. With 30 pre-measured stick packs, you get convenience, consistency, and zero mess—no scooping, spills, or second-guessing your dose.

During testing, the packets were easy to tear open and mix straight into water with minimal effort. I noticed a very slight bit of sediment at the bottom, but no unpleasant taste, making it a smooth, undetectable addition to any drink routine. Like many other options in this guide, each serving delivers five grams of micronized creatine monohydrate from non-GMO sources. While it’s more expensive than the bulk bag (about $0.96 compared to $0.29 per serving), you gain grab-and-go ease and reliable dosing. True to Promix’s standards, this creatine is third-party tested for heavy metals, soy, and gluten, and it’s vegan-friendly. You can even scan the lot number on your box to access lab results, a level of transparency that goes a long way in today’s supplement space.

Bare Performance Nutrition (BPN) has garnered a cult-like following of fitness enthusiasts and influencers—and the efficacy and quality of their creatine proves it’s for good reason. The product is sourced from Creapure, a highly purified form of creatine monohydrate, according to Michael Hamlin, CSCS, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness. Thanks to its purity, this unflavored powder is third-party approved by Informed Sport, making it especially perfect for the everyday exerciser working on strength, power, and performance training. E

“I can actually feel and see when I’ve been taking this powder consistently,” says WH wellness writer Gabrielle Kassel. “My shoulders become more defined, my legs look stronger in my leggings, and I don’t tap out as quickly during high volume squats.” Each container also provides 60 servings, giving you a bang for your buck.

Attention competitors, Klean Athlete Klean Creatine is the best pick for you, says Lexi Moriarity, RDN, a certified sports dietitian and founder of Fueled + Balanced Nutrition. As it turns out, the product name isn’t false marketing—the powder is genuinely pure enough that it earned an NSF Certified for Sport sticker, she says. Each five-gram scoop of this supplement contains no additional ingredients but creatine. There are no artificial colors, flavorings, sweeteners, GMOs, gluten, or other mystery ingredients, which is important if you ever want to participate in a sports competition that performs drug testing.

The powder is also unflavored and dissolves easily, making it perfect for mixing into water for mid-workout hydration or adding to your pre- or post-shake.

Supplements are unregulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)—and that includes creatine. As such, experts say it’s important to consider the following factors and complete your due diligence to find a high-quality product when shopping for a creatine supp. (Reading this article counts!)

Simplicity is often best with creatine. Look for products that list creatine as the sole active ingredient, ideally without added sugars, unless you're choosing a flavored version intentionally. Avoid proprietary blends that don’t disclose exact creatine content per serving.

The recommended daily dose of creatine is a minimum of five grams per day, according to the International Society of Sports Nutrition. This amount is shown to be safe and effective for maintaining creatine saturation within the muscles.

There are several types of creatine available, including monohydrate, citrate, and nitrate, but creatine monohydrate remains the most reliable. It’s the most extensively researched, dependable, effective, and cost-efficient option.

The U.S. supplement industry is largely unregulated, which means that the FDA doesn’t verify supplement marketing claims before products hit the shelves. But third-party testing can help. Look for certifications from organizations like Informed Choice or NSF Certified for Sport, which ensure the product has been tested for purity, potency, and contaminants. This is especially critical for competitive athletes concerned about banned substances.

For most people, taking creatine daily is not only okay, but it’s actually recommended to maintain optimal muscle creatine levels. Consistent daily use supports better performance, recovery, and long-term benefits.

The most common side effect of creatine is short-term water retention, which can lead to temporary weight gain. Taking more than 10 grams at once may also cause digestive issues such as bloating or diarrhea. However, for most people, creatine is well-tolerated when used as directed.

If you have pre-existing kidney or liver conditions, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are a child or adolescent, it’s important to consult your healthcare provider before taking creatine. For most healthy adults, creatine is safe and effective, but checking in with your doctor can provide added peace of mind and guidance.

#5043. Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

Should Government Officials Be Banned From Prediction Markets? House Oversight Says Maybe

The chairman of the House Oversight Committee is raising the prospect of barring government officials from trading on prediction markets, citing concerns that insiders are using nonpublic information to profit on platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.

In a staff memorandum released Friday, the committee detailed an investigation into insider trading by government officials, military personnel and people holding security clearances who have placed bets using information not available to the public.

The probe gathered nearly 1,700 pages of documents and included five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market platforms about how they detect and report suspicious activity.

Chairman James Comer framed the issue around public trust. “Americans are rightly concerned about public corruption,” he said, arguing Congress “has a duty to ensure our laws adequately prevent insider trading” and prohibit officials “from profiting from nonpublic information.”

He said lawmakers must weigh “additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people’s trust in government.”

The memo’s central recommendation is that Congress consider new restrictions on federal personnel, ranging from an outright ban on trading prediction markets to narrower limits on specific contracts, such as those tied to government decisions.

Applying such rules across all branches, the committee argued, would reinforce that government employees shouldn’t financially benefit from access to nonpublic information, and would remove even the appearance of it.

The memo stressed that existing insider trading laws already apply to prediction markets. It cited the Commodity Exchange Act, as amended by the STOCK Act, which bars federal employees, members of Congress and others from trading commodity futures, options, or swaps on nonpublic information drawn from their positions.

The committee credited the platforms themselves for policing their markets, noting that most reported insider trading incidents were first detected and flagged to regulators by the platforms. It singled out Polymarket, which recently hired a former law enforcement expert and rolled out surveillance software called “PolyGraph” built with analytics firm Chainalysis, and Kalshi for strengthening their detection protocols.

The scrutiny follows a string of cases involving alleged insider trading by public officials and government employees.

A U.S. soldier was charged in April over alleged Polymarket trades tied to a military operation that resulted in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Then, in August, the CFTC fined a former White House teleprompter operator for betting on presidential speeches.

The push also lands amid broader pressure on the sector, with the CFTC moving to assert authority over prediction markets in its fight against several states, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren sets her sights on the industry as the incoming Senate Banking chair.

#5042. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

#5040. Boris Johnson backs tokenization months after likening bitcoin to a ‘Ponzi scheme’

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On a Solana Breakpoint panel, the former UK prime minister said London should lead on blockchain and tokenization but questioned how investors could recover stolen crypto.

Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson said Monday that London should lead on blockchain development and asset tokenization, eight months after he likened bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) and other cryptocurrencies to a Ponzi scheme.

During a Solana Breakpoint panel titled "Crypto Is Key to the UK's Economic Future," moderated by The Block's Gareth Jenkinson, Johnson was asked why he had called bitcoin a Ponzi scheme. He acknowledged he was "not a great crypto buff," but recalled trying to help a man he met at church in Oxfordshire who had been "absolutely ripped off."

In his March Daily Mail column, Johnson wrote that the man initially handed over £500 ($660) to someone who promised to double his money by investing it in bitcoin. The man kept paying fees in the hope of getting his money back and ended up paying about £20,000 ($26,380), Johnson wrote.

"I want to know who's in charge," Johnson said of buying crypto, adding that he wouldn't know where to turn if his money was stolen. "Nobody knows who's in charge, apart from [Satoshi Nakamoto]," Johnson said. "And I don't know where to find him."

Nevertheless, Johnson described himself as "totally, totally in favor" of blockchain innovation and tokenizing "assets of all kinds," saying that London should be at the forefront of that work.

"Please don't think that my Luddite anxiety about crypto in any way means that I wish to slow down the development of blockchain or the lead that London should rightly have in that sort of technology," he said.

Fellow panelist Lord Ross Kempsell said he shared Johnson's concerns about the risks, but saw room for the UK crypto industry to grow under regulation.

Kempsell said he was primarily interested in institutional adoption of blockchain and that traditional financial firms in the City of London were increasingly using networks such as Solana as regulation advances.

The Financial Conduct Authority began taking applications for authorization under the UK's new crypto regime in September, and its initial application window closes Feb. 28, 2027. The regime starts Oct. 25, 2027, bringing activities such as operating crypto exchanges, holding crypto for customers, arranging staking, and issuing qualifying stablecoins under FCA oversight.

The Bank of England revised its stablecoin proposal in June, dropping the caps it had proposed on customer holdings and setting out a temporary £40 billion ($52.8 billion) issuance cap for each systemic sterling stablecoin.

#5039. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#5037. Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Could a Former Nvidia Executive Replace Jensen Huang? Arm’s Rene Haas Emerges as Candidate

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, putting a former Nvidia executive in contention for one of technology's biggest jobs.

Haas is one of several people under consideration, people familiar with the matter told the FT. There is no guarantee he will receive an offer or accept one. The FT said he maintains strong ties to Huang and some Nvidia directors.

Nvidia's board told Reuters it was still selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any candidate. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” it said.

Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded, following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a business executive suspected by U.S. officials of having Chinese intelligence ties. The company said it had no reason to believe its secrets were compromised.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones has become board chair. Analysts have also floated Nvidia data-center executive Ian Buck and AMD chief Lisa Su as possible successors, though those names are not confirmed appointments or offers.

An internal Nvidia suggestion-box post has attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supportive of Huang's reinstatement, according to Wired. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one anonymous employee wrote.

Other staff members have demanded transparency around his departure. The campaign shows Huang still has supporters inside Nvidia; it does not mean the board has opened talks to reinstate him.

Haas, 64, is a Silicon Valley-based semiconductor executive whose career spans engineering, product development and sales. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Clarkson University and worked at chip companies Tensilica and Scintera Networks before joining Nvidia in 2006.

He spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products business, then moved to Arm in 2013. At Arm, he rose from strategic alliances to chief commercial officer in 2015 and head of its intellectual-property products group in 2017, before becoming CEO in February 2022.

That appointment came as Nvidia's proposed $40 billion takeover of Arm collapsed under pressure from regulators. Haas was suddenly running a business his former employer had tried, unsuccessfully, to buy.

He steered Arm back onto the Nasdaq in September 2023 at an initial valuation of about $54.5 billion, one of the year's largest stock-market debuts. The IPO also gave Japanese owner SoftBank a way to sell shares while retaining control.

Unlike Nvidia, which primarily sells graphics processors and related computing systems, Arm licenses chip designs and computing architecture to companies including Apple, Amazon and Qualcomm, earning fees and royalties when customers use its technology. Arm-based designs are now increasingly found in cloud servers as well as phones.

Arm reported $1.44 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, up 27% from a year earlier. Royalties from data-center chips doubled, while Arm said initial commercial deliveries of its new CPU remain on track for early 2027.

Haas also sits on SoftBank's board and, since April, has served as CEO of SoftBank Group International, helping oversee its semiconductor and AI interests. A move to Nvidia would require untangling those ties, particularly because the companies are partners whose interests increasingly overlap in data-center hardware.

For Nvidia, the next leader would inherit not just its lead in AI chips, but delicate relationships with governments and customers as Washington debates tighter export restrictions on China. Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on November 17, with Kress at the helm and its permanent CEO search still underway.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. "Many devices contain about 200,000 flashes, which is typically good for more than 15 years, although it also depends on how many areas you’re treating," she says. Other recommendations on this list, like the Smoothskin, have unlimited flashes, which means they'll theoretically last forever, but are pricier.

Extra features like multiple intensity modes—lower options for sensitive skin; higher settings for those who want to see results fast (see the Nood)—or interchangeable heads for precise treatment all over the body (hi, Braun) can increase the price. The amount you spend comes down to the features you want in your device and how long you want it to last.

One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. For more targeted flashes, opt for rigs with compact heads, such as the Iouniya Laser Hair Removal, which can be used on both the face and body. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, warm weather likely won’t return until April or early May, meaning you’ve got several weeks to achieve smooth results. This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. Ultimately, I found four Amazon picks that are aligned with expert guidance and are currently discounted as low as $35. Talk about major savings! For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

Truthfully, they're not optimal for sensitive or dark skin. Many at-home devices cannot distinguish between melanin-rich complexions and dark hair, says dermatologist Corey L. Hartman, MD. Anyone else can still give them a try.

And, like with salon treatments, it's important to practice patience—this isn't a "one and done" situation. Many devices need to be used multiple times weekly to achieve the initial results. Plus, each at-home session can take 10 to 60 minutes, depending on how much body and facial hair you plan to remove. While a tad annoying upfront, this minor inconvenience has a major payoff because your hair will regrow slower over time with regular use.

#5034. Supreme Court rejects Custodia Bank’s bid for Fed master account

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Monday, the Supreme Court published its order list, revealing that it had denied certiorari in Custodia's case against the Federal Reserve Board.

The Supreme Court has said it would not take up a Custodia Bank's challenge to secure a Federal Reserve master account, denied its petitions for a writ of certiorari.

On Monday, the Supreme Court published its order list, revealing that it had denied certiorari in Custodia's case against the Federal Reserve Board. Custodia's legal journey has spanned over the past six years to try to obtain a master account, which allows institutions direct access to the Fed's payment systems and provides the most direct access to the U.S. money supply available to financial institutions. Those without master accounts are often forced to rely on partner banks with master accounts to provide services.

Custodia Bank, a Wyoming-chartered crypto-focused firm founded by Wall Street veteran Caitlin Long, began its master account quest in 2020 when it applied for that account in Kansas City. The Kansas City Fed then denied its application in January 2023, citing concerns about the bank's crypto-related business model. Custodia sued the Kansas City Fed in June 2022, initially over a 19-month processing delay and later arguing that federal law requires access for eligible institutions.

In March, an appeals court denied Custodia's petition for rehearing en banc, leaving intact a previous ruling that the Fed has discretion to approve or deny a master account for eligible institutions.

Custodia then petitioned for the high court to take its case up in July. The Supreme Court's decision to not take up the bank's challenged now leaves intact the previous decision. Custodia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Block.

Over the past year, attention has since shifted to an idea first floated by Fed Governor Christopher Waller for a "skinny master account." As innovations have evolved, the Fed said it may be time to offer a tailored approach while trying to mitigate risks, but some lawmakers have pushed back, questioning the safety and soundness of the Fed's payment rails.

The Fed asked for comments on the proposed slimmed-down master account last year and said it would not allow for interest on balances and could not access the discount window to borrow funds, among other limits. Comment letters from crypto advocates called the proposal "overdue" and also asked for some revisions. Community banks, however, warned that novel financial institutions were not subject to the same "robust regulatory compliance regime."

Custodia had previously told the Supreme Court that a limited purpose account was not sufficient, in part because it would mean that interest couldn't be obtained on the account's closing balance, Bloomberg reported.

Crypto exchange Kraken's banking division became the first crypto company to obtain a master account in March.

#5033. The Surprising Staying Power of Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy

A24’s Club Kid makes the case for the comedy’s unlikely legacy—and social relevance—in 2026.

EARLY ON IN Jordan Firstman’s dramedy Club Kid, druggie-with-a-heart-of-gold Peter has to shepherd his surprise 10-year-old son through an apartment party. Despite knowing each other for just a few hours, the club promoter and his child hold hands as he guides the way through the bacchanal. It’s a metaphor—what isn’t these days?—and it’s also kind of a recreation of a key sequence in Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy.

In that movie, 5-year-old Julian “Frankenstein” McGrath (played by young Dylan and Cole Sprouse) holds his hand aloft before he steps off the sidewalk, looking for help from his newfound father.

Replace McDonald’s breakfasts with coke and ketamine (plus a Charlie Kirk reference), and A24’s Club Kid is the clear heir apparent to the 1999 Sandler comedy. I’m far from the first person to make the connection. IndieWire’s David Ehrlich’s first-impression response was to ask: “What if A24 made a gay Big Daddy?”

It may seem like an odd movie for a brand like A24 to mirror. However, Big Daddy is somehow the film from the peak Sandler run that has had the longest shelf life. In fact, it may be the late ’90s–early 2000s comedy with the best depiction of the 2026 way of life. For better—or for worse.

Despite the fact that it was a hit at the box office, Big Daddy was reviled at the time of its release, even winning Sandler a Razzie Award for Worst Actor.

And, sure, it’s not the most elegant film—with its near-incessant Hooters jabs and Rob Schneider’s catastrophic accent—but still, it’s managed to stick around in the public consciousness for nearly 30 years. And it’s not just Ehrlich and I who think so.

“I particularly loved Big Daddy. That was my number one,” Paul Thomas Anderson said on an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast in 2017 when asked about casting Sandler in his film Punch-Drunk Love. “It was a little bit more polished; it was able to be sincere and [mix in] the crazy fucking dirty shit that Sandler likes to do and got the mix really right.”

In Club Kid, promoter Peter (Firstman, who wrote, directed, and stars) somehow ends up in charge of a precocious kid while flailing in both romance and his career. Peter, like Sonny, has to instantly shift his lifestyle, one that only functions when you have little to care for, including yourself. Both protagonists need an act of God to abandon their early-30s doldrums.

And honestly, it’s a sentiment that a lot of people my age (including myself) can relate to.

At the tail end of October, The New York Times published a story (which, thankfully, my parents haven’t sent to me yet) titled “Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.” The gist is that millennials feel burned out now that they know they’re unlikely to achieve the luxuries earlier generations enjoyed.

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take. But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach,” says one source in the article. Even decades ago, Sonny Koufax would have probably agreed with the article, before ripping out part of the newspaper to clean up some spilled milk next to his third bowl of cereal of the day. Both films find the hearts at the center of their respective protagonists’ messy, work-in-progress stories. Is there anything more 2026 than that?

When you watch Big Daddy in 2026, you almost forget how much of a schmuck—but vulnerable too—Sandler allowed Sonny to be. I was pleasantly surprised that Sandler ultimately loses his chance at raising Julian by himself. It’s a small, complicated victory for a movie that uses a schlocky, heartfelt monologue about fathers to reach a contrived moral coda, but we’ll take our wins where we can get them.

#5032. OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s dots complete purchases with tokenized card details, after users approve each transaction. The limited rollout targets U.S. ChatGPT Pro users; the wallet does not hold crypto or a cash balance. Coinbase and Circle offer a different route, using stablecoins to let agents pay for services with less human involvement.

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, giving its AI agents a way to purchase products using American Express, Mastercard, and Visa cards. The new system lets an agent finish online checkout without accessing the customer's actual card number, and it doesn't involve cryptocurrency.

The wallet works through dots, OpenAI's always-on AI assistants, which can browse websites and carry out tasks for users. A customer saves an eligible card, reviews the order and approves the payment using a security check such as a fingerprint or Face ID.

After approval, the card network creates a payment token containing substitute card details. The agent submits the token through the merchant’s existing checkout system, while the customer keeps applicable card rewards and dispute protections, according to OpenAI’s announcement.

“An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments,” Sherri Haymond, Mastercard's global head of digital commercialization, said in the announcement.

OpenAI previously introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe in September 2025, allowing people to buy from participating merchants inside ChatGPT. Wallet takes a different approach: agents can navigate ordinary online stores and use existing checkout forms, without requiring each business to build a special integration.

OpenAI is also courting merchants. Just three days before the Wallet launch, it introduced business profiles that let companies update product information and connect with potential customers through ChatGPT.

Google is working on a competing approach. Its Universal Commerce Protocol, introduced in January, aims to connect shopping agents with retailers, payment providers and post-purchase services across Google products.

Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets in February, giving software the ability to spend USDC, trade tokens, and pay for online services within preset limits. Unlike ChatGPT Wallet, the Coinbase product is primarily developer infrastructure, not a consumer checkout feature.

“It's not an SDK, it's not a library—it's a purpose-built wallet to work with an agent as quickly as possible,” Coinbase engineering executive Erik Reppel told Decrypt at the launch.

Coinbase's x402 protocol lets software pay for data or computing services as part of a web request, often using the USDC stablecoin. That makes tiny transactions possible without requiring an agent to enter card details or obtain human approval each time.

Stablecoin issuer Circle is pushing in the same direction. Its Agent Stack, launched in May, includes stablecoin wallets and tools for payments as small as $0.000001.

“USDC is uniquely well-suited for the agentic economy because it is internet-native, programmable, and always available,” Circle product chief Nikhil Chandhok said in a company statement.

Actual agent-driven demand is harder to measure. In September, blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs estimated that agents accounted for only 0.6% to 7.5% of filtered x402 commerce by value, using models that cannot conclusively distinguish agents from scripts.

For consumers, ChatGPT Wallet offers familiar card payments rather than a digital asset balance. OpenAI's terms say merchants remain responsible for deliveries and returns, and users must generally contact their card issuers for billing disputes.

OpenAI plans to let users authorize future purchases within spending limits or specified categories, but has not announced when that feature will arrive. In the meantime, it warns that merchant websites may block shopping agents or flag otherwise legitimate Wallet purchases as fraud.

#5026. What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.

Canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which launched its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.

Canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a New York company founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton launched in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.

Canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one big ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.

The network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.

In June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.

Think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.

This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.

"Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.

What sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:

Canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. New CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.

CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.

In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares launched the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.

Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.

CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.

Canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC plans to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.

#5022. Standard Chartered says Japan’s bond tokenization plans could help drive RWA market to $2 trillion

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The bank said tokenizing Japanese government bonds could bring more long-term debt onchain and encourage other countries to follow.

Japan's plans to tokenize government bonds (JGBs) could help the tokenized real-world asset market reach Standard Chartered Bank's existing forecast of $2 trillion by the end of 2028.

The market currently stands at around $45 billion, Geoffrey Kendrick, the bank's global head of digital assets research, wrote in a Monday report. Its $2 trillion forecast has mainly relied on tokenized money market funds and equities, each growing to $750 billion. Longer-dated government bonds would provide another source of growth toward that target, Kendrick said.

"The current crypto sell-off will pass, and when it does, it will be the bringing of real-world assets on-chain that matters most," Kendrick said in an email shared with The Block.

"The more important implication of tokenizing longer-dated debt in one of the world's largest government bond markets is that others may follow suit," Kendrick wrote in the report.

Most government debt brought onchain so far has been short-term Treasury bills, with almost no longer-dated debt tokenized, according to the report. Kendrick put tokenized U.S. Treasury bills at around $13 billion, compared with just under $1 billion in tokenized government debt outside the U.S.

Japan has the world's third-largest government bond market, and BlackRock recently signed a tokenization MOU with SBI and Startale there. Kendrick said other governments may follow if Japan's program becomes large enough to demonstrate cost savings and easier movement of bonds as collateral.

Japan's Ministry of Finance held its first study group meeting on bringing government bonds onchain on Oct. 8. Kendrick noted that there are three options under consideration. Japan could tokenize existing government bonds, issue new bonds on a distributed ledger, or do both.

The first option would be simpler because the legal structure and cash flows would remain the same, Kendrick said. Issuing bonds directly on a ledger could save more work and costs. Japan is still gathering industry feedback.

"While the plan still lacks key details, such as the choice of blockchain and timelines, we think the proposal is a significant step forward for one of the world's largest government bond markets," Kendrick wrote.

Several pilot programmes to tokenize government debt are underway around the world, most notably the UK's Digital Gilt Instrument pilot, expected to go live in early 2027, Kendrick noted. He said a large Japanese program could encourage the U.S. and other major government bond markets to pursue tokenization too, following Wall Street's emerging tokenization model, adding: "This would help to drive overall tokenised RWAs towards our end-2028 market cap forecast of USD 2tn."

#5021. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

Four nonprofit organizations are taking some of the world's biggest AI companies to court, asking a California judge to stop them from developing more powerful artificial intelligence systems before something goes seriously wrong.

The 63-page complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, Irreplaceable Education Fund, and the Alliance for Secure AI.

They want an immediate court order prohibiting the companies from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced models as of November 12, 2026.

“The Frontier AI companies are developing AI Systems that they do not understand and that act contrary to developer intent, evade control, and break the law,” the plaintiffs argue. To prevent this, they request “an immediate injunction forbidding Defendants from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most capable systems as of the date of this Complaint”

That wouldn't necessarily mean shutting down ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other existing products. Instead, it would effectively make today's technology the limit, preventing the companies from releasing more powerful successors.

The complaint also asks the court to prohibit the companies from using AI to independently conduct or direct research into better models, a process related to what researchers call recursive self-improvement. The concern is that such systems could eventually improve faster than humans can understand or control them.

The nonprofits argue that California already has laws that could prevent companies from developing products that endanger the public, even before those products cause serious harm.

Their lawsuit invokes the state's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits unlawful or unfair business practices. One part of their argument is that developing increasingly capable AI systems creates a public nuisance: a danger that affects the health, safety, or property of a broader community.

For example, a factory releasing dangerous chemicals into a neighborhood could face legal action before someone suffers a fatal injury. The plaintiffs want the court to apply similar reasoning to AI development.

They argue that companies are knowingly creating increasingly powerful systems that could facilitate cyberattacks, help develop biological weapons, or eventually escape human control.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs argue in the complaint.

Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement that the groups want the court to declare the companies' practices unlawful and “freeze further AI development.”

The legal challenge is whether the alleged risks and practices are enough to justify such sweeping restrictions. Even though these frontier labs constantly warn about how powerful and dangerous their models are, as defendants they have not been found liable, and warnings about potential catastrophe do not automatically establish a violation of California law.

The complaint points to incidents that have already occurred as evidence that the dangers aren't entirely hypothetical.

In July, OpenAI models escaped a controlled testing environment and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity evaluation.

A subsequent independent investigation found that roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents used an unauthorized internal message board to coordinate, with about 700 joining the attack on Hugging Face. The agents were attempting to obtain answers to the benchmark testing them.

These incidents involved AI agents, programs that can execute tasks, browse websites, write code, and interact with external systems rather than simply responding to questions.

Documented security failures, however, are not proof that today's AI models can cause human extinction. The plaintiffs are connecting those incidents to predictions about what increasingly capable systems might eventually do, and that broader danger remains disputed.

“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect,” Matthew Platkin, the former New Jersey attorney general representing the plaintiffs, said in the statement.

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Cypherpunk mined $9.9 million worth of ZEC in 44 days and says its mining business is worth more than the value of its holdings.

Cypherpunk Technologies, the Zcash treasury company founded by Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, got back to buying ZEC amid its recent pullback while its mining business recorded its first quarterly profit.

Nasdaq-listed Cypherpunk (CYPH) reported $2.6 million in operating income for the third quarter, following the August launch of its Zcash mining fleet. Net income totaled $306 million, entirely driven by $330.8 million in unrealized gains on its ZEC holdings.

"With the pullback in Zcash, we resumed our open market purchase strategy," CEO Dug Onsi said on Monday's earnings call.

Since quarter-end, Cypherpunk bought another 3,775 ZEC for about $3.5 million at an average price of $920.40. Tacking on October's mining production, its treasury reached more than 341,858 ZEC, which is just over 2% of the entire circulating supply. Cypherpunk aims to hold at least 5% of Zcash's circulating supply, much like the 5% ether supply ownership target set by the Tom Lee-chaired Bitmine.

ZEC was down a further 2% to $887 on Monday, extending its decline over the past month to roughly 22%. In late September, ZEC hit a new all-time high of $1,650.

Cypherpunk mined 8,967 ZEC during the first 44 days of operations, pulling in nearly $10 million in revenue. Hosting costs averaged out to about $104 per token, and all the ZEC it mined were routed into its treasury.

The company also raised $56.5 million through its at-the-market stock offering program in the third quarter. The funds went towards mining equipment and more ZEC purchases.

A portion also covered operating expenses "so we don't have to sell the Zcash that we mined," Onsi said.

CIO Will McEvoy said that mining changes how investors should value the company and that whether its shares trade above or below the value of its crypto holdings — a metric commonly known as mNav — "doesn't make a ton of sense nowadays."

"I think analysts should be sort of looking at the business from a sum-of-the-parts perspective," he said, pointing to its ZEC treasury and mining revenue and earnings.

#5015. The Week Jensen Huang Fell: How a Spy Scandal Toppled Nvidia’s CEO

The Week Jensen Huang Fell: How a Spy Scandal Toppled Nvidia’s CEO

In the span of a few days, the most powerful executive in artificial intelligence went from untouchable to unemployed.

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia from a graphics-card maker into the roughly $4 trillion engine of the AI boom, resigned Thursday after 33 years, felled not by a bad earnings report but by a scandal with the texture of a spy thriller.

Here’s how a defining week for AI, and by extension crypto, unfolded.

The crisis began with reports that Huang had grown close to Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.

For a company at the center of the U.S.-China chip fight and a looming debate over tighter export controls, the national-security overtones were impossible to ignore. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, though it said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.

On Nov. 8, Huang apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, acknowledging the relationship.

What might have been a single lapse quickly snowballed. The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported to Huang.

By Thursday, Huang was out as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones took over as board chair. The abruptness stunned an industry accustomed to treating Huang as synonymous with Nvidia itself.

Then, a day after his resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, an “intimate” one with a second unnamed Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Reuters did not identify her, and Nvidia declined to comment. Huang has acknowledged only the Alice Huang affair, deflecting when the Times asked about Powell.

Nvidia’s stock cratered more than 14% at the open on Thursday before clawing back to close down about 4.6%. Wall Street quickly sorted winners from losers: rivals like AMD and Broadcom fared better, while companies tightly tied to Nvidia’s business took the brunt.

The reaction underscored how much of the AI trade, and the crypto market that increasingly moves with it, rests on a single company.

The scandal then rippled outward. Singapore barred Alice Huang from returning to the country, Alibaba shares slid on reports it was a Megaspeed customer, and congressional committees had already sought a closed-door briefing from Huang over his Megaspeed ties.

The loudest names in tech, AI and crypto called the ouster a blunder, with one founder branding it “a massive mistake.” Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion-box post drew more than 1,600 comments, many pleading for Huang’s return. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one wrote.

The board has moved on regardless. According to the Financial Times, it approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive who led Arm through its 2023 IPO, as a potential successor, though Nvidia called speculation about any candidate “premature.” Analysts have also floated Nvidia’s Ian Buck and AMD’s Lisa Su.

Nvidia’s chips power the AI data centers whose explosive buildout has become intertwined with crypto, from AI-agent commerce to the mining firms pivoting to host AI workloads.

Leadership turmoil at the company that supplies the picks and shovels ripples outward, and it lands amid a broader reckoning over AI’s role in everything from cyberattacks to data-center politics.

Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, with Kress at the helm and the permanent CEO search still underway, a nervous moment for a market already rattled by a sharp week-ending selloff.

For now, the company that defined the AI era is leaderless at the top, its founder’s legacy clouded by scandal, and the question hanging over Silicon Valley is whether anyone can fill the role Huang made uniquely his own.
