Pourizaee adds that the contoured footbed helps keep feet aligned and relieves foot strain. While I often wake up with sore feet that hurt as soon as I step out of bed, I find that when I’ve worn this slipper the day before, foot fatigue is next to zero.

If you like a cozy slipper, the Gemma II delivers. I have the cream color, which is made with a wool upper that keeps my feet warm and looks cute with all my cold-weather loungewear. Other styles have a faux-fur or flannel upper, which also looks super warm and cozy. Plus, since the slipper is designed for indoor and outdoor wear, the synthetic outsole is ultra-durable with a patterned tread design. I’ve even gone for post-rain walks with my dog on wet pavement, and never felt like I was going to slip.

Overall, this slipper is warm, cozy, and ultra-cushioned. It keeps my feet happy with the plush feel underfoot, and I love keeping it by the door when I need a cute shoe to slip on fast.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The Ortho-Cushion system (which includes the removable orthotic insole, ergonomic sole, and fitting spacers) helps to customize the fit and level of cushioning and support. I didn’t realize before selecting my normal size that Orthofeet recommends ordering a half-size down for a more snug fit, but placing the smallest blue fitting spacer (1/16 inch) under the insole kept my foot feeling super secure. Even without any customization, I was impressed by the high level of cushioning that hugs my arches and feels really nice under my heels. The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. That shape propels you forward with each step and also helps take some pressure off the joints. Plus, the EVA outsole also has lots of traction patterns to keep every step feeling stable and secure.

I also love the faux fur lining and insole that feels super cozy and keeps my feet warm even while walking outdoors on chilly mornings. The suede outer adds to that cozy vibe and looks super cute. I initially wasn’t sure if this slipper would be my style, but I find myself reaching for it all the time when I leave the house for quick errands and coffee dates with friends. I have the taupe color and often pair it with ankle jeans and sweaters for a comfortable fall fit.

While it does run slightly small, the brand offers half sizes, and the slipper comes with customizable features, so I didn’t find it an issue at all. However, if you’re concerned about fit, I recommend ordering a half size down.

The Sunday Mule Slipper from Bombas is perhaps the most stylish casual shoe that I own. The elongated, oval-toe shape looks super chic, and it's wrapped entirely in a fluffy sherpa material for that cozy-yet-put-together feel. Whether I’m couch-rotting on the weekend, grabbing a latte, or taking a casual stroll around town, I can always count on this slipper. It looks great with a wide-leg lounge pant or leggings with slouchy socks, but I’ve also worn it with a cropped pair of jeans.

Sharkey says it's a good cozy and comfortable option, and that Bombas did a great job with the level of cushioning. That’s thanks to the memory foam footbed, which has a nice squishy feel, contours to the shape of the foot, and softens impact with every step. That contouring feature does wonders for making sure the slipper stays on, even while trekking all around town. However, Sharkey says the backless design does tend to slip off the feet if you’re not careful. I haven’t had any issues there, but it’s something to keep in mind if your feet need an ultra-supportive shoe—in which case, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper might be a better choice.

The rubber outsole gives this slip-on shoe a major upgrade, since it helps provide traction when I wear it outside. I keep this slipper mainly for wearing around the house or quick errands, but I have worn it during short, casual walks without worry. The fluffy sherpa material, inside and out, makes it a super cozy option for lazy days cuddled up on the couch and keeps my feet warm even when I take it for a spin outdoors.

Plus, there’s plenty of chic color options. I went with the cream, which I find pairs well with almost anything in my closet—but there’s also a black and brown for additional neutrals, and a dusty purple or tomato red option for something more bold. While this slipper from Bombas might not be the most supportive option, I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a plush, super stylish slipper.

Clogs get a bad rap for making your feet sweat, slide around, and (sorry!) being kind of ugly. But this slip-on clog from Rothy’s nails it on the style front, and is also durable, breathable, and super comfortable. The Casual Clog is well-loved by me and executive editor Abigail Cuffey—oh, and Sharkey recommends it, too.

This slipper/clog hybrid is made with the brand’s signature cushioning made from recycled water bottles and arch support that Sharkey says is ultra comfortable. She also says she likes that the heel cup is a bit deeper than your standard slipper, which helps with stability. I find that the deep heel cup helps cover the back of my foot, so it doesn’t slip off when I’m running around the house doing laundry or walking up and down stairs. The outsole is also made from recycled water bottles and has a grooved design that makes it super durable with tons of traction. I usually wear it for casual outings and meeting up with friends, and find it looks great with baggy jeans and sweaters for a casual-yet-put-together look.

While I own the merino wool version, Cuffey owns both the merino wool and hemp styles. She’s been wearing the hemp clog since fall 2024, and loves that the ultra-cushioned footbed molds to her feet. “It feels like a hug for your heels and toes,” she says. She wears it as a lounge shoe and an outdoor shoe, because of the grippy outsole and substantial feel. Cuffey’s thoughts on the merino wool clog are generally the same, but she loves that the wool feels a little cozier while still airy and breathable. “I usually go through slippers so fast because they get so gross, but Rothy’s Casual Clogs are the first ones that have staying power in my closet,” she says.

It does run a little wide, but the fabric is stretchy, so I haven’t had any issues with it feeling too loose on my feet. But if you’re in between sizes, Rothy’s recommends sizing down for a better fit.

The L.L. Bean Wicked Good Moccasin has become my favorite ever since I got it in the mail. A moccasin is a slipper made of soft leather that wraps around the foot with a single gathered seam at the front. This style is the cushiest, coziest, most supportive I’ve ever worn, earning a permanent spot in my fall and winter footwear rotation.

Unlike some moccasins, Pinker says this style feels especially stable thanks to the rubber outsole with added grip and traction. Plus, the suede material is more structured than other moccasins I’ve worn, which makes for a snug, secure feel. I’ve worn this moccasin weekly over the past month, and I can tell it’s extremely durable. The suede has a lot of heft, and combined with the hand-stitched construction, this moccasin stands up to wear and tear. The fur lining is also extremely comfortable and warm, and I love wearing this shoe on colder days to keep my feet toasty. The insole is also made from the same fur material, which delivers a super plush, cushioned feel underfoot.

There’s also plenty of fur lining the outside of the slipper, which I find super stylish, along with the rawhide laces and bow. It looks great with both joggers and wide-leg sweatpants, and I even wore it recently with cuffed jeans and a boxy sweater for a casual brunch. I have the brown pair, but with seven shades to choose from (including blue, red, and purple!), there’s no shortage of styling potential.

One note: this slipper is spot-clean only, unlike others that can go in the washing machine. However, I wear it nearly every morning lately to walk my dog when the ground is still dewy, and I haven’t gotten any stains that took more than a quick pass with a dry washcloth to remove.

I desperately needed a new house slipper a few weeks ago, so I decided to snag this pair from Fulton—and I couldn’t be happier with my decision. While you could totally get away with wearing this slipper outside (it’s super cute and definitely sturdy), I love keeping this pair inside and free from outside germs—IYKYK.

At first, I honestly wasn’t sure this pair would be a winner: the footbed was super uncomfortable the first day that I wore them. It felt like all the raised areas were in the wrong places, which made it a little difficult to walk. Had I known then that the Fulton website explains there’s a 10-hour break-in process, I’d have been way less concerned.

Lo and behold, by the following day the slippers felt much better—and only continued to get more comfortable as the cork footbed molded to the exact shape of my foot. I wouldn’t call this slipper plush by any means (though the wool upper is quite cozy), so if that’s what you’re looking for, the Ugg, Dearfoams, Orthofeet, or L.L. Bean styles might be better options. But this shoe makes my feet feel so good.

I’ve been suffering from some pretty gnarly foot pain from recently developed plantar fasciitis, but since I started wearing this slipper around the house every day, my feet feel brand new. My arches and heels feel way less achy throughout the day, and it no longer hurts to plant my feet on the ground first thing in the morning.

If you prefer a slide over a slipper, this pick from Oofos is perfect. I often bring it to the gym to wear in the locker room, sauna, or on the way to my post-workout smoothie spot, and the cushy foam insole feels great on my achy feet. As our WH 2025 Fitness Awards winner for Best Recovery Shoe, I had to test it myself for this guide.

Pourizaee says this slide is ideal for recovery or all-day wear thanks to its excellent shock absorption and built-in arch support. That’s because it’s made from the brand's signature OOfoam technology—a springy EVA foam that has plenty of cushion and feels nice and squishy underfoot. The insole’s contoured shape creates built-in arch support, with a high mound near the center that fits perfectly under the arches. That shape reduces stress on the knees, ankles, and other joints. My ankle pain (from a previous sprain) and mysterious knee pain definitely feel better when I wear this slide regularly around the house. Plus, the deep heel cup keeps my foot anchored in place, even when I’m doing housework at lightning speed.

WH executive health and fitness director, Jacqueline Andriakos, swears by it for managing her foot pain, too. "My podiatrist told me I had to get a pair for work-from-home days and going to and from barefoot workout classes," she says. "I notice my chronic foot pain is light years better when I’ve been wearing it more regularly."

Another perk? The foam is water-repellent, odor-resistant, and machine washable. The only feature that would make this slide better, Pinker says, is an ankle strap for extra stability and support.

The right cushioning absorbs impact from walking on hard surfaces to help prevent foot pain, says Pourziaee. All of our favorite slippers have at least a medium level of cushioning.

I’m a shopping writer covering style for Women’s Health. I’ve written guides to the best white t-shirts, most comfortable sneakers, best walking shoes, and more. I also test footwear (including slippers and slides!) constantly.

#4983. CFTC backs blockchain-based derivatives infrastructure as Backpack, tZERO win approvals

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig said the agency had approved the applications, marking another sign of its increasingly crypto-friendly regulatory approach.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to establish regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that use blockchain technology to execute and settle transactions.

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig highlighted the approval of a blockchain-based derivatives exchange and clearinghouse, which appears to correspond to Backpack's newly announced U.S. regulatory approvals.

"These approvals mark an important milestone in the evolution of American financial markets and demonstrate that there is a regulated pathway for a new generation of market infrastructure built using blockchain technology," Selig said.

Financial tech company tZERO received its exchange approval last week, following its earlier approval from the agency to operate a derivatives clearing organization, which it says will allow the firm to "support derivatives trading and clearing through its own regulated entities."

"The approvals establish a unique new derivatives market infrastructure vertical within tZERO's growing Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) business, enabling the company to develop exchange and clearing services for financial institutions and other market participants," tZERO said.

Backpack announced its approval from the CFTC on Monday. In a statement, Backpack US President Mark Wetjen called the approvals a "really big deal."

"This is an achievement that demonstrates that the highest standards of regulatory compliance and blockchain innovation can go hand in hand," Wetjen said.

Over the past year, the CFTC under Selig has taken significant steps for crypto regulation, including working with the Securities and Exchange Commission to clarify which digital assets are securities or commodities, creating an innovation task force and supporting 24/7 trading and bitcoin perpetuals.

Selig, who currently serves as the CFTC's sole sitting commissioner, could soon have fellow commissioners. Last week, President Donald Trump tapped Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to be commissioners at the CFTC. The Senate Agriculture Committee will hold its nomination hearing for the bipartisan pair on Tuesday, after which their nominations could head to a full Senate confirmation vote.

#4979. We Found the Best Adjustable Dumbbells for Every Home Gym

Looking to make more gains while taking up less space? These picks from SMRTFT, PowerBlock, and REP Fitness pack a big punch in a small package.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF THERE'S ONE piece of home gym equipment anyone can make room for at home, it's a pair of adjustable dumbbells. These clever pieces of fitness gear require minimal space, shifting from light to heavy with a quick turn of a knob or tweak of a setting. They simplify things by tackling two challenges of working out at home: space and equipment. Think about it: A single pair of adjustable dumbbells can replace around 15 standard dumbbells.

"There's a reason dumbbells are in every single big-box gym," says MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., who created an arm-focused muscle-building program, All Out Arms, based heavily around dumbbells. "If you want targeted muscle—and that’s what all guys want—then you want dumbbells." Adjustable dumbbells (just like adjustable kettlebells) offer a range of weights from one compact footprint, eliminating the need for multiple sets of weights.

If you prefer working out at home (or do so out of necessity on days when you can't make it to the gym), a pair of adjustable dumbbells is a solution that helps you stay consistent with your training without leaving your home. These are effective pieces, especially when combined with cardio equipment and a great weight bench. Check out our top picks for the best adjustable dumbbells for your home gym right now.

"The Nüobell is the best blend of reliability and authentic dumbbell feel I’ve used," says Samuel, who has been using these for over three years. "The shape and design of these 'bells make them ideal for accessory motions, like skullcrushers and biceps curls, and they’re easy to hold for goblet squats too." Aside from a few scratches, they've held up great to three years of heavy use.

With a maximum weight of 80 pounds of weight per dumbbell and a feel that's nearly indistinguishable from traditional dumbbells, users can utilize the same set of weights for a complete full-body workout. Users can quickly drop down to lower weights for exercises like bent-over flies or pile on the plates for more intense squats. "It features a 'turn-and-click' design rather than just a built-in selector," notes Williams. Users simply turn the handle until they reach their desired weight.

During testing, Howell noted that the Nüobell arrived assembled and was easy to plug-and-play once unboxed. Of all the adjustable dumbbells he tried, these felt the most like actual dumbbells. "These feel like the next evolution of the traditional dumbbells we have become used to in gyms," Howell said.

The major defining features include: metal plates and handles, top-tier construction, easy click-and-go weight adjustment, and the selected weight displayed on the dumbbell itself.

However, Howell expressed some concerns about the rack it came with, feeling it might have been an afterthought. He questioned whether the tempered plastic rack would withstand the constant re-racking of the metal plates over time. Nevertheless, he emphasized that the actual dumbbells are well-crafted and feel solid as hell.

In Howell's opinion, these dumbbells are best for someone who has invested in a home gym and is serious about fitness. They are tailored for the hardcore client who likely has a squat rack and barbell in their garage as well, but wants to add an elite set of adjustable dumbbells to their training arsenal. If you’re building the mother of all home gyms and money is no object, this comprehensive premium set of dumbbells from SMRTFT might just be your best pick.

These BowFlex adjustable dumbbells adjust from 5 to 52.5 pounds in 2.5-pound increments, which replaces up to 15 pairs of dumbbells (that’s a lot of potential time and money saved). We love that the weight distribution is close to that of traditional dumbbells, and the 2.5-pound increments offer more customization in weight ranges. No matter how these BowFlex dumbbells are ordered, they arrive at your door in two separate, well-packed boxes.

The weight is adjusted through selection dials located on either side of each dumbbell. The dial system is easy to use, though not exactly as streamlined as SMRTFT's single-twist mechanism. Keep in mind that changing the weight requires docking and adjusting both sides of each dumbbell–that’s two dial adjustments for each change in weight. But I prefer them to PowerBlock dumbbells.

The previous version of the SelectTechs had a plastic casing, but these updated models now feature premium metal components that are better protected from damage. We find the design a bit wide and cumbersome for certain exercises, such as triceps extensions. "In my experience, these work best for chest-supported rows and overhead presses," says Samuel.

These dumbbells have been in regular use in my garage for half a year, I haven't had any issues with wear or tear. That said, it's essential to handle them with care and consider your exercise preferences when incorporating them into your home gym setup. Like most of the dumbbells on this list, it's probably not a great idea to drop these on the floor after finishing a set.

The last note is that advanced lifters may feel a little constrained by the 52.5-pound max weight and may want to consider the 90-pound-max-weight BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 1090s instead.

Read More: Our Review of the BowFlex Results Series SelectTech 552 Dumbbells

The NordicTrack Select-A-Weight Dumbbells are sturdy and easy to use, featuring metal plates and a robust plastic casing designed to withstand the occasional drop (though we don't recommend it). With a weight range of 10 to 55 pounds per dumbbell, adjustable in 2.5-pound increments, they cater especially well to home workouts. However, they're not our top pick for accessory movements due to their relatively broad plates.

This set arrived assembled and was ready to go once unboxed. "I appreciated that it came with a tray that gave it a home and an easy-to-store footprint," noted Howell. "Making changes in weight by 2.5-pound increments was fairly easy, and they felt really sturdy and safe even when adjusted to heavier loads—the knurled metal handle helped with this."What Howell didn't love about these was that there was no way to confirm what weight you were using once the 'bells' were removed from the rack. Only the rack is labeled with weight numbers, not the actual dumbbell."I think this is an ideal product for someone who knows their way around a gym and is looking for a solid addition to their home to supplement," says Howell. "They're perfect for an intermediate client."

In terms of sound, while "these are quieter than other adjustable dumbbells on the market, they make more noise than the PowerBlocks," explains Samuel. Additionally, if you wish to incorporate barbell movements into your home workout routine, we've found that these dumbbells work seamlessly with the Hyperbell.

One of my favorite equipment makers, I was surprised how long it took REP Fitness to come out with a viable adjustable dumbbell option. But it seems like they were waiting to create something special, and that's what they've done with the QuickDraws.

The plates can be adjusted in 2.5-pound increments, spanning from 5 to 30 pounds. For those heavy lifters, 30 pounds might not be enough, but for the average user looking for a quick pump in the arms or lighter weights for perfect accessory movements, this is a great pick. For anyone who wants to increase the weight, REP Fitness offers heavier options with the same streamlined design, for up to 60 pounds.

They've patented their Lock-N-Load adjustment system, which is straightforward and lets you change the weights by flipping a switch on each dumbbell. This system allows you to swap weights quickly, so you can change the load between dumbbell exercises and avoid stalling.

For our testing, the dumbbells arrived in two boxes and require minimal assembly, making them an ultra-accessible choice for delivery and home use.

PowerBlock adjustable dumbbells are an ultra-sturdy set designed for lasting performance, perfect for executing heavy-duty moves like dead stop rows, Romanian deadlifts, and heavy presses. At just 12 inches long with the storage stand, these dumbbells offer decent compactness and versatility.

The Pro 50 Adjustable Dumbbells cover a weight range of 5 to 50 pounds per dumbbell, with adjustments in increments of 2.5 pounds. This weight range suits beginners well, and more experienced lifters can expand the weight by opting for additional expansion kits. For those who find 50 pounds per dumbbell insufficient, PowerBlock offers heavier models such as the Elite USA (up to 90 pounds per dumbbell) or the Pro 100 EXP (up to 100 pounds per dumbbell). Most models of adjustable dumbbells by PowerBlock feature the same pin-and-lock adjustment mechanism, which is easy to use and avoids jamming issues found in some other systems.

In his testing, Howell pointed out the compact structure of the actual dumbbell, noting the plate-like weights, which are more like weighted frames than traditional circular ones. Howell found this design "genius", as the square nature of the dumbbell makes it easy to lay down once done using it without it rolling away or requiring a rack to rest it in. He also appreciated that they arrived assembled and were fairly easy to unpack and begin using.

However, Howell expressed concerns about the durability of certain components, such as the handles and the "clip" that allows you to lock your chosen weight in, which are made of plastic. He believes these dumbbells might not be robust enough for consistent use, particularly for hardcore gymgoers.

Despite these concerns, Samuel praises their adjustability and durability, stating, "I've never encountered a more durable adjustable dumbbell. I love them for farmer’s walks, heavy DB lunges, and thrusters, and rely on them anytime I do a metcon-style workout at home." Samuel also shared he’s dropped these from three or four feet up after tough sets of incline presses, "and they hold up just fine." (Although it's not advisable to make a habit of dropping any adjustable dumbbells regularly.)These dumbbells feature comfortable contoured handles that enhance grip during workouts. However, they do not provide the same weight distribution as traditional dumbbells, as Samuel points out: "If you’re looking to use a set of adjustable movements for plenty of accessory movements, go with something more dumbbell-shaped."

Look for a weight range that meets your fitness goals. Most adjustable dumbbells can be adjusted in 2.5- or 5-pound increments, so it's important to consider a weight range that fits your needs.

Adjustable dumbbells come in different shapes and sizes. Consider the size and shape of the dumbbells and make sure they feel comfortable in your hands. Basically, does the dumbbell feel "good" or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference and might involve some trial and error.

Some adjustable dumbbells distribute the load differently than traditional dumbbells (atypical), changing how it responds to certain movements (particularly accessory movements). A good rule of thumb is if you're looking to perform heavier exercises (farmer's carries, RDLs, rows) you can consider an adjustable dumbbell that doesn't distribute its weight like a traditional dumbbell, such as the PowerBlock option featured above. If you're planning to do more accessory movements (like biceps curls or skull crushers), opt for a traditional dumbbell-shaped option.

There are a few different mechanisms adjustable dumbbells use to switch weights, with some being easier or more user-friendly.

This mechanism uses a dial on the end of the dumbbell handle to adjust the weight. To change the weight, you turn the dial to the desired weight, and the mechanism will lock in the appropriate weight plates. Some adjustable dumbbells must be docked in their storage base to change weight using a dial, while others can be adjusted outside their docking station.

This mechanism uses a pin to select the desired weight and can take some practice to get used to if you're new to it. To change the weight, pull out the pin, select the desired weight, then reinsert the pin into the corresponding slot to lock it in.

This mechanism uses a twist-locking mechanism to secure the weight plates. To change the weight, you twist the handle to unlock the weight plates, remove or add weight plates, and then twist the handle back to lock in the new weight.

Warranties reflect a manufacturer's confidence in its product. And with some of the best adjustable dumbbells priced at or above $500, you want to be sure your investment is protected. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous five-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including adjustable dumbbells. To build this guide, I tested more than 30 adjustable dumbbells over the past five years, drawing on my experience and that of my fellow MH fitness editors, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. Samuel utilized the top-performing adjustable dumbbells featured in this guide in fitness programs with several of his advanced clients.

We also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn, to test and assess how well these dumbbells performed in the real world (read: a high-traffic training facility). In addition, we sought insights from trainers from both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity class for further anecdotal and experiential perspectives on the top adjustable dumbbells.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including durability, weight distribution, ease of shifting between weights, and aesthetics. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: explosive exercises (such as cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (such as bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory movements (such as biceps curls and lateral raises). All dumbbells were also dropped from a standard bench to test baseline durability (no adjustable dumbbell should ever be dropped from shoulder height), and they were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

Adjustable dumbbells pack a ton of perks compared to regular dumbbells, with the most obvious being their space-saving design: No matter which adjustable dumbbells you choose, you can guarantee they'll take up less space than the sets of traditional dumbbells they replace.

Another attractive benefit of adjustable dumbbells is that they're more cost-effective than multiple sets of traditional dumbbells. A lot of the options on this list aren't exactly budget buys, we know. But building out a weight rack with 5-15 sets of high-quality traditional dumbbells can add up in cost even quicker.

This comes down to three things: space, personal preference, and how you plan to use your dumbbells. If you have unlimited space, you can definitely consider standard dumbbells.

"If you're building out a home gym and especially if you like to train accessory motions and work through a full range of motion, you still can't beat standard dumbbells," explains Samuel.

"They're going to be more durable, have better weight distribution for most moves, and, as cool as some adjustment dial might be, there's nothing more efficient than literally putting a 35-pound dumbbell down and picking a 40-pounder up."

But if you're in tight confines or like to work out on the go, opt for a good adjustable option. "You can load a pair of Powerblocks in your trunk much more easily than you can load 10 pairs of dumbbells for a road trip."

You'll also want to consider how often you'll drop your dumbbells. Even the best, most durable adjustable dumbbells on this list still have weight-switching mechanisms and won't hold up to being routinely dropped from a few feet in the air after a set of shoulder presses as well as standard dumbbells.

The weight of adjustable dumbbells depends on your fitness level and goals. Typically, they come in two main categories: those that max out at around 50 pounds per dumbbell and those that start at 50 pounds and get way heavier.

For beginners and folks looking to engage in moderate strength training at home, a set that maxes out at 50 pounds per dumbbell should suffice. They offer a range of weights for a wide variety of exercises and are a great starting point. Beginners can work on everything from biceps curls to overhead presses to squats with these.

Now, if you're a seasoned lifter, powerlifter, or someone aiming to build strength, opt for a pair of adjustable dumbbells that can go well above 50 pounds per bell. Adjustable sets from SMRTFT can offer a max of 80 pounds and 100 pounds per bell, respectively. For experienced lifters, added weight means greater versatility in tackling heavy exercises and challenging yourself.

Just like standard dumbbells, adjustable dumbbells are safe when used correctly and with proper form. But, as with any type of fitness equipment, there are some safety considerations to keep in mind.

It's important to choose adjustable dumbbells that are well-made and constructed from durable materials. If you're using an old-school model with removable plates, make sure they're securely attached to the handle before you start your lift.

The shape, feel, and weight distribution of adjustable dumbbells can take some getting used to, depending on the model you're working with. Because they may feel different compared to standard dumbbells in movements you do regularly, it's important to focus on slow, controlled movements and proper form throughout your workout (especially as you acclimate to them).

#4977. Ledger Brings Clear Signing to Solana, Ending 'Blind' Signing for Jupiter Swaps

Ledger Brings Clear Signing to Solana, Ending 'Blind' Signing for Jupiter Swaps

Ledger has brought clear signing to Solana, allowing users of its hardware wallets to read exactly what they are approving before they sign a transaction.

"Until now, most Solana DeFi on a Ledger meant signing blind," the company tweeted on Monday. Users can now verify a swap on decentralized exchange aggregator Jupiter "in plain words, showing what you send and what you get before you approve," it said.

Would you approve a swap you can’t read?Clear Signing is finally live on Solana. Until now, most Solana DeFi on a Ledger meant signing blind. Now you can verify a Jupiter swap, in plain words, showing what you send and what you get before you approve.

Clear Signing now covers… pic.twitter.com/BuW3m7y5GG

Blind signing, in which users approve transactions displayed as unreadable data, has long been a weak point for hardware wallet users, since it leaves them unable to spot a malicious request. Ian Rogers, Ledger's chief human agency officer, likened it to "signing a blank check" in a presentation at Solana's Breakpoint conference.

A Jupiter swap that previously meant scrolling through 13 hard-to-read screens on a Ledger device now takes three, showing what the user is giving, what they're getting and who they're dealing with, Rogers said. "It's a huge step for every Solana user," he added.

Clear signing now covers nine Solana apps and 18 of the 22 most common actions users take on the network, according to Ledger. It was built with the Solana Foundation and Anza, the developer of Solana's Agave validator client, with Jupiter and lending protocol Kamino as the first supported apps.

Rogers also pitched the company's tools for AI agents. Ledger's approach is that an agent "never holds the keys; you do," he said, comparing it to a teenager who has to ask parents for the family car. The agent requests approval when it needs to move funds, and the user signs off on a Ledger device.

Because that means an agent has to stop and wait, Ledger last month launched Agent Intents, a single queue where approval requests collect so agents can keep working while users approve them when convenient. It works with Pay.sh, a service that lets AI agents pay for APIs on Solana, Rogers said.

He also showed off Ledger Atom, the touchscreen device based on Android's open-source code that Ledger announced last month. When it's time to sign, the device switches its screen to Ledger's secure chip, so secrets stay hidden from Android, Rogers said. Atom will be the first hardware beyond the Solana Seeker phone to carry the Seeker platform, bringing its more than 1,500 apps to the device, he added.

Ledger has previously teamed up with MoonPay on tools to let users control AI agents' crypto spending with its hardware wallets.

The launch comes weeks after Ledger investigated a suspected $87 million drain of user funds, which it later said was tied in all confirmed cases to a reseller, Cryptobilis.

#4976. Coinone warns of phishing, identity theft after customer data breach

The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.

On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records. Coinone said it learned about the breach in the same day.

According to Coinone, the information potentially exposed names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, national identification numbers, home and wallet addresses and transaction IDs.

Coinone said the affected data varies by customer, and people who never contacted its support center were unaffected. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

The exchange urged customers who shared passwords during support interactions to change them and warned that fraudsters could impersonate Coinone using details from previous conversations.

Coinone said its account, trading and wallet infrastructure operates separately from MetaM’s servers, with no evidence of direct compromise. The exchange said it has reported the incident to South Korean authorities.

The disclosure comes as South Korea moves to strengthen financial-sector cybersecurity. In October, the Financial Services Commission identified security deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial firms reviewed.

On Thursday, the regulator said it would allow crypto exchanges to suspend withdrawals when hacking is suspected, alongside calls for round-the-clock monitoring.

#4968. Enterprise blockchain is going to come back from the dead

Opinion by Paul Brody, founder and chief executive, Nightfall Networks

Do you remember Pets.com? It raised $110 million from Amazon and others to build a business where people ordered pet toys and dog food online.

The company crashed and burned, and everyone learned an important lesson: you can’t profitably ship a 50-pound bag of dog food to a customer’s door.

As online retail entrepreneur Ed Baum asked in a 2001 postmortem: “Did Pets.com’s business plan assume the invention of transporters to magically move bags of pet food without shipping costs?”

Please, whatever you do, don’t share this with the people at Chewy; they might not realize their business model doesn’t work. Chewy reported $12.6 billion in sales and $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year.

The real lesson of Pets.com wasn’t that shipping dog food was a bad idea. It’s that the idea arrived before the logistics, customer habits and unit economics required to make it work.

As it was with chew toys and dog food, so it may be with enterprise blockchains.

Collectively, the crypto industry probably incinerated just as much money trying that between 2017 and 2023 as Pets.com. Maybe more. But the dozens of companies that went after enterprise blockchain were not delusional; they were just too early.

It’s not hard to understand the appeal of enterprise blockchain solutions, at least superficially. Nearly all enterprise systems today tend to fail at the boundaries between companies. There are two failure modes: mode 1, the OG failure mode, where collaboration information is constantly out of sync.

In this world, enterprise IT systems are islands, communicating asynchronously with each other by digital text messages and emailed spreadsheets. It’s cheap and easy to set up, if you don’t mind always having slightly wrong information.

Failure mode two is the costly, real-time proprietary integration. Powerful industry leaders politely request their key suppliers and partners to join their closed but always-on networks.

Chewy reported $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year. Source: Chewy.

These are very costly, but they work well and leave everyone with a kind of business version of Stockholm syndrome, where you come to appreciate the thoroughness and efficiency of the digital choke-hold you are in.

Blockchains offered a better path forward: shared information and business logic across an open ecosystem. All the benefits of a proprietary system in terms of real-time visibility and efficiency, without the lock-in.

Sometime around 2017, this started to look like a very obvious good idea. Investment poured in, consortia launched, press releases were drafted and released, and then pretty much everything crashed and burned. TradeLens, We.Trade, Contour, B3i, ASX Chess, Everledger. All came and went in just a few years.

No company wants their competition to see what they’re doing in detail. Mostly, this meant building a private/permissioned chain and then doing lots of non-blockchain-like things to it and in it to try to keep information private. The results were uniformly slow and expensive and failed to gain traction.

It’s hard to understate the bloodbath of companies and startups that tried and failed to make enterprise blockchain work. A quick web and history search turned up 18 different ones, some of them well-known.

What few survivors of this are left have “de-chained” themselves — giving up the blockchain theater and reverting to a classic software-as-a-service (SaaS) model. Many companies that tried and tested these permissioned enterprise systems as users came away from their experience with a clear learning: we tried blockchain, it didn’t work.

That’s unfortunate because everything is different now.

Blockchains have scale. Ethereum in 2020 handled 1 million transactions a day and costs per transaction periodically spiked to $30-50 when demand was high. Today, most transactions get done under a penny and capacity is ramping toward billions of transactions a day. Nobody talks about the “trilemma” anymore. Ethereum is decentralized and it is scaled.

Related: Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade launches on Sepolia testnet

Finally, there’s the money. It’s all moving onchain. Regulators around the globe have blessed stablecoins and the result is a tsunami of liquidity, with transaction volume reaching almost $1.8 trillion in June.

If we combine the operational benefits of blockchains with the financial ones, we get something that enterprises have never really had before: a single ecosystem where you can not only buy, sell, and move assets, but get paid for them as well.

There was just under $1.8 trillion in adjusted stablecoin transaction volume in June. Source: Visa

The return on investment from every single component of this equation is big. Combined, they can yield colossal advantages. McKinsey partners even found that digital supply chain tools could make inventory reductions of 35-75% possible through better planning.

More conservatively, from my experience in the field, just switching away from the existing cascades of spreadsheets and electronic data interchange (EDI) messages can allow firms to run most supply chains with about 20% less inventory at the same service level. That’s worth billions in working capital in most industries.

It gets better from there. Smart contracts reduce the time required to handle many business contract rules from days to minutes and cut the costs of administration in half.

Microsoft began moving its Xbox video game network onto smart contracts for handling royalties and cut the time to access monthly royalty statements from 45 days to four minutes. All that while handling more than 2 million transactions a day.

And once you have inventories, contracts, purchase orders and invoices onchain, you can go after working capital directly as well.

When you can prove your purchase order originates from a top-quality buyer, you can access credit for less. And when you have full visibility into inventory and delivery status, you can factor receivables immediately and efficiently.

The possibilities and the returns are big. The use cases are obvious. It’s time to try again.

#4965. 'Nobody Knows Who's in Charge': Boris Johnson Stands by Bitcoin Skepticism at Breakpoint

'Nobody Knows Who's in Charge': Boris Johnson Stands by Bitcoin Skepticism at Breakpoint

Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson is sticking to his doubts about Bitcoin, telling a room full of crypto developers that he still can't see who is in charge of the world's largest cryptocurrency.

"As far as I can see, nobody knows who's in charge, apart from Yakimoto Nakasori, and I don't know where to find him," Johnson said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London, deliberately mangling the name of Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. "If six billion got stolen from some cryptocurrency, I wouldn't know who to apply to, or how to get the money back. That's my problem."

Johnson was asked about a column he wrote in March for the Daily Mail, in which he called Bitcoin a "giant Ponzi scheme." The column drew pushback from the crypto industry, including Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor, who tweeted that Bitcoin has no issuer, promoter or guaranteed return.

Bitcoin is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi requires a central operator promising returns and paying early investors with funds from later ones. Bitcoin has no issuer, no promoter, and no guaranteed return—just an open, decentralized monetary network driven by code and market demand.

— Michael Saylor (@saylor) March 13, 2026

On stage, Johnson admitted he is "not a great crypto buff" and holds little, if any, crypto himself. His view was shaped by a man he met in his Oxfordshire village who had lost thousands and kept paying more in the hope of recovering his losses, he said. "If the search for the greater fool had reached the wilds of South Oxfordshire, then probably there was something not quite right about this thing," Johnson said.

He also questioned the name itself, noting that "crypto" comes from the Greek for "hidden." "I don't think it's a good sell to tell people that this thing is concealed," he said.

Johnson drew a sharp line between Bitcoin and the technology behind it. "Please don't think that my Luddite anxiety about crypto in any way means that I wish to slow down the development of blockchain, or the lead that London should rightly have in that sort of technology," he said. When it comes to blockchain and tokenizing assets, the UK has "got to be at the forefront," he added.

Moderator Gareth Jenkinson, head of multimedia at The Block, pushed back when Johnson suggested Bitcoin was valuable to drug dealers, arguing that blockchains are far more traceable than cash. Asked by Johnson who guarantees Bitcoin, Jenkinson replied: "No one has to guarantee it. That's the beauty of the protocol."

Lord Ross Kempsell, a Conservative member of the House of Lords who previously worked for Johnson, said more than 8% of UK adults now hold some form of crypto asset, and that institutional adoption of blockchains is growing in the City of London. That ownership figure has fallen, however: the Financial Conduct Authority's latest consumer research, conducted in August and September 2025, found 8% of UK adults own crypto, down from 12% in 2024, though still double the level in 2021.

The UK is "on the precipice of creating a lot of regulation" for the sector, Kempsell said, pointing to the FCA's work on its regulatory perimeter and the Bank of England's coming stablecoin framework. "I share Boris's anxieties about the risks," he said, but within that perimeter, "there's a lot of scope here for a high growth industry."

In June, the FCA finalized its rulebook for crypto firms ahead of a mandatory regime due to take effect in late 2027, days after the Bank of England eased its stablecoin rules, scrapping planned individual holding caps in favor of a £40 billion issuance limit per coin. The Bank has since been handed a legal duty to foster stablecoin innovation, and it has set out a shared vision for tokenization with the FCA.

Kempsell also argued that being outside the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation allows the UK to set its own rules for crypto. The EU itself is set to revise MiCA in 2027 to cover foreign stablecoin issuers.

Bitcoin bottomed after the US midterm elections in 2018 and 2022 — and the great Bitcoin crash of November 2026 looks like history repeating. Bitcoin plunged more than $10,000 this week, and is currently trading at $65,116 for a 12.4% loss.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao rebuffed the idea that Binance is behind the crash. “No, Binance did not sell crypto. I bought crypto in the past few days,” he said. He attributed the crash to money shifting to the Anthropic IPO, the Bitcoin ETF outflows, security fears about crypto in general in the wake of the Binance hack, and hot inflation data raising expectations of interest rate hikes. Bitcoin fell to a four month low near $62,000 on Sunday but has since rebounded above $65,000. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 10, which is Extreme Fear.

The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang is plotting a comeback to the top job at Nvidia with allies, following a determined push in Silicon Valley to pressure the board to reinstate him.

Nvidia shares plunged after Huang resigned as CEO and from the board on Nov. 12, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress named as interim CEO. The resignation came shortly after news broke he’d had two other affairs, including one with a subordinate.

Multiple people confirmed Huang has been discussing the idea of returning with confidants, even though an independent probe by the board is examining allegations he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy who helped ferry chips to China.

On Wednesday, the group outlined “pqai27,” a proposed roadmap that aims to protect Ethereum against threats from quantum computing and artificial intelligence.

At Devcon, researcher Justin Drake said he hopes to complete the transition in 2028 while the published roadmap still targets December 2029.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses. Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist. The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30.

#4960. 6 Best Travel Dresses of 2026, Tested by a Style Writer and Travel Expert

Our top options are from Uniqlo and lululemon.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The best travel dresses are the kind you can throw in a carry-on, forget about for hours, and still slip on looking put-together. As a style writer who’s constantly on the move (I checked off eight countries last year alone), I don’t say that lightly. I’ve learned the hard way which pieces wrinkle beyond the help of a hotel room iron, feel restrictive mid-transit, or just don’t pull their styling weight once I land. The ones worth packing work just as well with sneakers as they do with sandals, and make getting dressed in an unfamiliar place easy.

I tested 30-plus styles in real-life conditions, paying close attention to how they pack, wear, and hold up after long days of travel. The best ones strike the sweet spot between comfort and style with breathable fabrics, packable silhouettes, and just enough versatility to earn their spot in my very limited luggage space.

I’ve packed the below dresses for trips to Cancún, Paris, Marrakech, St. Lucia—and plenty of destinations in between—putting them through everything from long-haul flights to full-day itineraries. These are the ones I’ll reach for no matter where I’m headed next.

The Uniqlo Ultra Stretch AIRism Dress rings in at under $40, but the quality feels far more luxe. It’s smooth, polished, and super easy to style in a variety of ways for a single trip—meaning I can wear it multiple times without anyone clocking a repeat outfit.

The fabric is where this dress really shines, IMO. The signature AIRism material is made from 100 percent polyester, making it lightweight, breathable, and quick-drying with a soft, stretchy feel that moves with me. Whether I’m dealing with humid temps or long travel days, it keeps things cool and comfortable without clinging.

It also nails that easy, flattering fit-and-flare shape. It’s more fitted through the bust and subtly flares out toward the legs, creating a flowy drape that I especially love when walking—it just moves beautifully. The midi length hits at about mid-calf, striking that sweet spot between casual and pulled-together, so you can dress it up or down without overthinking it. I wore this dress to Barcelona during a warm September, and the breathable material and loose fit made it a major win.

And if you’re worried about packing a longer dress, don’t be. It packs down incredibly well, and any wrinkles from being in a backpack or suitcase shake out quickly before heading out the door. Plus, it has pockets! A huge win for travel days when you want to easily stash your phone, sunnies, or room key. The only downside: It’s unlined, so the white version is slightly sheer. But that also adds to its airy feel, and there are plenty of other color options if you want more coverage.

The updated lululemon Align Dress is a sporty option that can truly do it all. Designed with yoga in mind, it’s incredibly breathable, stretchy, and sweat-wicking—but doesn’t look overly athletic, thanks to its sleek, sporty-chic silhouette. It transitions seamlessly from a morning flow to a full day of sightseeing, making it one of those rare pieces I always throw into my suitcase.

The updated version improves on the original Align Dress with a nylon base and even more elastane, giving it more stretch and wrinkle resistance—yes, even after being packed down in compression cubes. Just like the brand’s famed Align leggings, this fabric feels ultra-smooth and lightweight.

Fit-wise, it features an A-line silhouette, meaning it's more fitted through the torso and gradually flares out toward the hem for a flattering drape. The mini length hits at about mid-thigh, keeping things cool and unfussy. Thoughtful built-ins like a shelf bra for light support and attached shorts with pockets make this dress perfectly practical and polished while on-the-go.

From a packing and styling perspective, it’s a no-brainer. The shorter length and featherlight fabric make it easy to toss into your suitcase and unpack with minimal wrinkles. I’ve styled it casually with a baseball cap and my fave travel shoe (shoutout to the Dr. Scholl’s Time Off Sneaker), but it also dresses up surprisingly well with a kitten heel and dainty jewelry. The only real downside is the price—it’s one of the most expensive picks on this list—but considering the quality, performance fabric, and versatility, it’s worth the investment (watch out, as it’s often on sale).

Stylish, short-sleeve dresses under $100 can be surprisingly hard to find. That’s why the Free People Blaine Midi Dress is one of my new faves. It offers just enough coverage (especially if your shoulders tend to burn in the sun like mine) while still keeping things breezy and cool. The overall vibe leans laid-back with that signature Free People look—think relaxed and boho but still put together.

Made from 100% cotton, the fabric is soft, breathable, and especially comfortable in heat and humidity. What I really love, though, is the subtly textured, crinkled finish paired with dramatic pleating, which keeps wrinkles at bay.

The fit is intentionally loose and billowy, giving it that airy, floaty shape the brand is known for. That said, its breezy fit means it runs large. My usual size worked, but I ended up using waist-cinching clips to create a bit more of a fitted shape, so I definitely recommend sizing down. It’s a midi-length dress that hits a few inches above the ankle, with thoughtful details like a stylish keyhole cutout at the back, and, yes, pockets.

This dress definitely leans casual, but in the best way. It’s great for daytime outings, exploring a new city, brunch, or even throwing over a swimsuit. I recently packed it for a trip to Mexico and it held up beautifully in the heat and humidity—easy, breezy, and styled perfectly with a simple sandal and a crochet bag.

This long-sleeve dress gives just the right amount of coverage on the arms but excels at breathability. That makes it perfect for everything from long-haul flights or bus rides to cooler evenings. It feels light and airy without sacrificing style, with an easy silhouette that still looks thoughtfully put together.

The fabric is a standout: a soft, gauzy 100% organic cotton that feels breathable and gentle against the skin. Like the Free People dress, it has a naturally textured, crinkled finish, so it doesn’t show wrinkles, even after being packed. Instead of pleating, it features a flouncy, tiered skirt with horizontal seaming, which adds movement and a bit of playful volume.

Fit-wise, it leans relaxed and slightly oversized, so sizing down is a smart move if you want a more tailored look. The mini length hits mid-thigh, creating a fun contrast with the long sleeves, while details like the subtle bell sleeves and button-down front upgrade the look. It’s one of those dresses that looks just as good styled casually as it does dressed up a bit.

It’s also incredibly versatile. The lightweight cotton makes it comfortable enough for daytime exploring while the longer sleeves give a little extra coverage when the temperature dips. It’s easy to throw on with sandals during the day or dress up with boots or jewelry at night—and just as easy to pack, thanks to that forgiving, wrinkle-resistant texture.

Meet the perfect mini dress. I own it in black, and it always looks incredibly chic—whether I’m dressing it up with heels for a city dinner or keeping it casual with sandals for daytime plans. It’s one of my favorite pieces because it feels polished no matter how you style it—coming in clutch for travel.

The fabric plays a big role in that versatility. It's made from a polyester crepe that has a subtle texture and is naturally wrinkle-resistant—ideal for tossing in a suitcase without a second thought. It holds its shape well and doesn't cling, giving it a clean, streamlined look straight out of your bag.

It has a classic, body-skimming silhouette that gently follows your shape without feeling tight or restrictive. The mini length hits at about mid-thigh, while the boat neckline adds a classy feel that instantly upgrades the overall look. It’s simple, but in that very polished, well-designed way.

It checks all the boxes for travel. The Bond Dress packs down easily, comes out looking polished, and can be styled in multiple ways depending on your itinerary. If there's a downside, it's that the streamlined fit doesn't leave much room for built-in functionality like shorts or roomy pockets, but the trade-off is a sleek, goes-with-anything mini you’ll reach for again and again.

The Dylan Mini Dress earns its spot as the most stylish pick thanks to its ultra-flattering shape and the prettiest range of colors and patterns. It has that slightly romantic feel that instantly dresses up your outfit, whether you’re heading to dinner or just wandering a new city. I always get compliments when I wear this dress (it was a major hit during my trip to Mallorca)—and it looks just as good in photos as it does in person.

The fit is where it really stands out. It has a flattering scoop neckline trimmed with delicate lace, plus a fitted bodice that dips slightly at the waist to help elongate your torso. From there, it flows into a long, airy skirt that moves beautifully as you walk. Adjustable straps let you customize the fit, and the built-in bra with removable pads adds support without the need for extra layers—always a win when packing light.

In terms of length, it hits a few inches above the ankles for that easy, breezy feel, and it comes in petite, regular, and tall options so you can find your ideal fit. The longer length gives it a slightly dressier edge, while still feeling relaxed enough for daytime wear. Despite the longer length, I don’t have any issues packing this dress in my suitcase when I pop it into a packing cube.

Style-wise, it leans pretty and girly in the best way. It’s perfect for summer travel or warm-weather destinations, but also transitions nicely into cooler conditions with a simple cardigan layered on top. The only con? Popular colors and patterns tend to sell out fast—so if you see a style available in your size, I recommend snagging it ASAP.

Since traveling involves lots of packing, travel expert Addie Bell says to look for wrinkle-resistant materials like spandex, nylon, or polyester. These fabrics are great for maintaining a polished look after being packed in a suitcase. Travel days often include a lot of walking, so you'll also want to make sure your dress's fabric is breathable—cotton and linen are great choices, but they are prone to wrinkling.

If you’re only traveling with a carry-on or trying to maximize storage, stick to neutral tones like black, navy, white, and beige, which are versatile and easy to mix and match with other wardrobe pieces. "Subtle patterns can also help hide wrinkles and stains, making the dress more travel-friendly," says Bell. But bright colors can add a fun, vibrant touch. "I always recommend sticking within a similar color palette to ensure they match other items you’re bringing.”

#4958. DTCC, Barclays Say Tokenization's Real Prize Is Unlocking Idle Collateral

DTCC, Barclays Say Tokenization's Real Prize Is Unlocking Idle Collateral

The biggest payoff from tokenizing traditional assets won't come from simply putting them onchain, but from putting idle collateral to work, according to executives at the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) and Barclays.

"You can tokenize an asset, but if you can't do anything with it, what's the point?" Val Wooton, DTCC's global head of equities solutions, said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London. "For me, it really is around collateral and liquidity."

Scott Lucas, head of digital assets at Barclays, agreed. A lot of collateral sits "relatively idle" at central securities depositories, he said, and much of the early value for banks will come from moving it more efficiently between their own accounts, before extending that to clients. "There's a lot of money in good housekeeping," he added.

The pair spoke on a panel days after DTCC announced that its tokenization service will connect to Solana, with tokenized assets expected on the network in the second half of 2027.

The service, which launched on October 28, can tokenize assets held at DTCC's depository, starting with Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasury bills and bonds, Wooton said. The tokens carry the same legal and economic rights as traditionally held securities, and adding Solana reflects DTCC's strategy of being "open," "interoperable" and "multi-network," he added.

Wooton said the biggest opportunity lies in "liquidity optimization," which he said could save "millions, if not billions" of dollars by letting firms move assets that are currently stuck when markets are closed.

Large financial institutions today over-fund and over-collateralize every day because they treat collateral as "just in case," he said. Moving assets onchain, around the clock, would let firms manage collateral "just in time," freeing up "a significant amount of balance sheet" to put to other uses. He added that the ability to move assets and settle them atomically could be "extremely powerful" in times of market stress.

Lucas pointed to Barclays' participation in DTCC's tokenization launch last month, one of the bank's first public moves into the space, and described the efficiency gains from managing its own collateral as good housekeeping.

Barclays is also working with Ironlight on tokenized structured products, Lucas said, though he stressed "it's not a done deal." He added that he would like to see Solana adopted by other central securities depositories around the world, building a shared infrastructure layer across Asia-Pacific, Europe and the United States.

Both executives said adoption remains early. Wooton said the industry is "still in the crawl stage," and that traditional and digital rails will exist side by side "for quite a long time," though DTCC's clients are already tokenizing assets daily.

Lucas said he tries to stay "healthily skeptical" about the speed of adoption while making sure Barclays is ready for its clients. At a recent traditional finance conference in Miami, he said, "every institution we met had money on the table," making investments and building products, a shift from a year earlier, when most were still asking questions.

Barclays has been gradually expanding its crypto activities. The bank invested in U.S. stablecoin startup Ubyx earlier this year and has reportedly weighed a push into tokenized deposits and stablecoin payments, according to Bloomberg. It was also among the investors backing crypto custodian Copper in 2022.

#4953. Luxor CEO warns of AI ‘dark forest’ following Bitcoin miner hijack

Attackers redirected customers’ Bitcoin mining power through Luxor’s Commander platform over the weekend, prompting its CEO to issue a warning to crypto businesses.

Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor has warned that AI-enabled cyberattacks are becoming increasingly difficult to defend against after attackers compromised its mining-management platform and redirected customers’ computing power to another mining pool over the weekend.

In an X post on Sunday, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen said the attack came through a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector,” without specifying how AI was used in the attack, warning that these types of attacks will only get more frequent over time.

“At this moment, anyone running any sort of substantial business, especially in crypto, is inundated with AI-enabled attacks,” Hansen said in an X post. “This does not seem to be slowing down; rather, it’s speeding up as models get better and more attackers enter the arena.”

The warning comes as security researchers have documented the spread of AI-assisted hacking tools, raising the prospect of faster attacks against businesses holding money or controlling valuable infrastructure.

“Abliterated models are running 24/7 against your entire surface, looking for a little crack, which they then use to (almost instantly) expand,” added Hansen.

Hansen said Luxor has had to put the majority of its feature work on hold in order to harden its cybersecurity. The company has also acquired its own GPUs to run unrestricted open-weight AI models aimed at improving its security posture.

“I urge anyone running a similar service to do the same.  It’s your only defense in this new AI-powered dark forest. ‘The only thing that stops a bad guy with a gun is a good guy with a gun.’”

Initial reports suggested that about 64,000 mining machines representing 13 exahashes per second were redirected to the OCEAN mining pool on Saturday.

Luxor has not confirmed either figure, saying the incident affected just over a dozen customer accounts using its Commander mining-management tool.

Luxor said it patched Commander within two hours of detecting the unauthorized changes and began restoring affected machines to their original pool settings. It pledged to compensate customers in full for the redirected mining power and publish a post-mortem.

Cointelegraph contacted Luxor for comment.

Related: Coinone warns of phishing, identity theft after customer data breach

“We have explored the issue extensively, and it was isolated to the Commander tool. None of Luxor’s other services (including Luxor Pool and LuxOS) were affected,” said Luxor.

Initial reports suggested the attackers received no mining rewards. However, a Bitcoin address identified by CoreX as associated with the incident subsequently received two OCEAN payouts totaling approximately 0.162 BTC, worth about $10,500.

Hansen’s warning follows a string of reported AI-assisted intrusions targeting crypto businesses.

Earlier this month, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that a group called Crafty Falcon was using AI-powered tools to attack financial companies, including cryptocurrency exchanges, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed in October that an attacker used what it called “offensive agentic techniques” to access its systems. The breach exposed password hashes, live tokens and other customer information.

Anthropic said in a September report that multiple groups had developed “automated exploit foundries” with AI, accelerating the pace of vulnerability research, testing, and exploit design.

#4952. Solana Drops 'Mainnet Beta' After Six Years: Here's What 1.0 Is All About

Solana Drops 'Mainnet Beta' After Six Years: Here's What 1.0 Is All About

Solana is officially out of beta, more than six years after launching a blockchain that has been handling real money the whole time.

The Solana Foundation on Monday retired the “mainnet beta” label and introduced Solana 1.0, a shared version number for the network's underlying rules. The change is primarily about how developers and validator operators coordinate software updates, not a fresh boost to transaction speed or any other meaningful improvement over what users already have.

Solana launched its mainnet beta on March 16, 2020, and kept the experimental-sounding name even as users traded tokens, built applications, and moved assets across the chain.

Nothing happens to those assets now. “Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same,” the Foundation said. Users don't need to swap tokens, move wallets or install anything to keep using the network.

Solana has two major validator clients: Agave, developed by Anza, and Firedancer, built independently by Jump Crypto. Each has its own code, release schedule and version numbers, which can make it harder to tell whether different software releases support the same network features.

Solana 1.0 creates a common reference point for the protocol itself. An Agave release and a Firedancer release can support the same protocol version without sharing a software version number.

That distinction matters as the network relies on more than one software implementation. A bug in one client need not affect every validator, although software diversity alone cannot guarantee the network will stay online.

“Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once,” the Foundation warned. Operators still need to check whether their particular software supports a planned upgrade and follow its activation instructions.

The Foundation said it coordinated the change with Anza and the Firedancer team. Its announcement does not describe a new voting system or a change in who governs Solana; the network's governance process for proposals remains separate.

The Foundation credits engineering work that preceded Monday's announcement, particularly Alpenglow and Firedancer. Solana's Alpenglow upgrade went live on October 21, replacing the system validators had used to reach agreement since launch.

Alpenglow targets transaction finality of roughly 150 milliseconds, compared with about 12.8 seconds previously. Finality is the point at which a transaction is considered settled; that improvement came from the October upgrade, not from calling the network 1.0.

Firedancer also reached mainnet in 2025, giving validators a separately developed alternative to Agave. That reduces dependence on a single codebase, though the extent of the protection depends on how widely different clients are actually used.

Solana has reasons to be careful with promises of reliability. Its network went offline for nearly five hours in February 2024, following an outage lasting almost 19 hours a year earlier.

Documentation and block explorers will gradually adopt the new mainnet name, according to the Foundation. Its upgrade tracker still lists Agave 4.4 as planned for November and Agave 4.5 for December, each with its own release and activation requirements.

#4950. Asian chip stocks tumble ahead of Nvidia Q3 earnings

The weakness came amid a wider sell-off in regional equity markets, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 2% and South Korea’s Kospi losing 2.6%.

Asian semiconductor stocks slid on Monday ahead of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings, with analysts set to look for signs that the AI spending boom remains on track amid uncertainty over the chipmaker’s leadership and future growth.

Japanese chip-testing equipment maker Advantest (6857:TYO) dropped about 10.4%, semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec (6920:TYO) declined more than 10.7% and chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron (8035:TYO) fell 5.7%, according to Google Finance.

South Korean memory-chip makers Samsung Electronics (005930:KRX) and SK Hynix (000660:KRX) lost 5.8% and 4.2%, respectively, while Taiwanese chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (2330:TPE) slipped 3.8%.

The broad decline could reflect caution toward AI-linked stocks ahead of Nvidia’s results, although the weakness came amid a wider sell-off in regional equity markets, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 2% and South Korea’s Kospi losing 2.6% as of 4:04 am UTC.

Nvidia is scheduled to release its fiscal third-quarter results on Tuesday, followed by an earnings call. The results will be Nvidia’s first since founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

Investors and analysts will be looking at how Nvidia will respond to the AI demand boom while its leadership is in turmoil. Morningstar on Friday said it will be looking to see whether the mid-term elections have led to any concern about future demand and whether Nvidia’s outlook for the industry has changed.

In August, Nvidia forecast fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, excluding any data center compute revenue from China.

Related: CoreWeave stock jumps 15% premarket after Q3 revenue beats estimates

Analysts expect Nvidia to report slightly higher quarterly revenue of $109.3 billion, including $101.8 billion from its data center business, according to Visible Alpha consensus figures published by S&P Global Market Intelligence on Thursday.

S&P Global said revenue expectations had risen since the previous quarter on anticipated strength in Nvidia’s Blackwell chips.

Morningstar analysts also said they expect another “beat-and-raise quarter” out of Nvidia, given strong capex trends among hyperscalers and enterprises.

“We’d be stunned if Nvidia provided an earnings miss or weak forecast,” they said.

Nvidia shares closed Friday down 2.01% at $162.85, according to Google Finance.
