#4929. Singapore, Germany test cross-border FX settlement with CBDCs

Project Simbolon aims to reduce the cost and time of cross-border settlement and promote common standards for payments and FX

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Deutsche Bundesbank used wholesale central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) to test settlement of euro–Singapore dollar trades across their separate digital asset test environments.

As part of Project Simbolon, the two central banks used payment-versus-payment settlement, meaning the final transfers of each currency depended on the final transfer of the other, MAS said in a Monday press release. Zero-knowledge proofs allowed each system to verify whether settlement conditions were met without directly integrating the central bank ledgers.

The project aims to make cross-border transfers between Singapore and Germany faster and cheaper. It also aims to promote common standards for cross-border payments, foreign exchange and securities transactions tied to tokenized assets.

The test was the first milestone under a November 2025 memorandum of understanding between the two central banks on tokenization and cross-border settlement. It also advances broader efforts to make tokenized financial markets more efficient under Project Guardian, a tokenization initiative MAS launched in May 2022.

“Project Simbolon paves the way for eliminating settlement risk in global foreign exchange transactions,” said Sabine Mauderer, first deputy governor of the Bundesbank.

In September, the Eurosystem launched Pontes, a system that lets financial institutions settle wholesale tokenized asset transactions in central bank money.

#4928. Fed Is Modeling AI 'Super Intelligence' Scenarios, Including Job Losses and a Stock Market Slump

Fed Is Modeling AI 'Super Intelligence' Scenarios, Including Job Losses and a Stock Market Slump

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Monday that central bank staff have started modeling how artificial intelligence could reshape the U.S. economy, including scenarios where the technology raises unemployment even as the economy grows.

Speaking at the Fed's Productivity and Jobs conference in San Francisco, Warsh described three possible paths: a productivity boom benefiting workers, a boom that leaves workers behind, and an AI investment bust that drags down stocks and economic growth.

“These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts,” Warsh said, explaining that staff are using simplified economic models to test what might happen over the next several years. The Fed is preparing for different outcomes, not predicting which one will materialize.

Warsh called the technology “super intelligence,” or SI. That language is now official Fed terminology after an October change following a Donald Trump administration executive order, rather than a scientific determination that today's AI systems have already surpassed human intelligence.

In the most optimistic scenario, AI helps companies produce more with the same resources, raising the country's economic output above its historical growth rate. Workers share in those gains, and unemployment stays close to the level economists associate with a healthy job market.

In the second scenario, AI still makes the economy grow faster, but businesses automate jobs more quickly than displaced workers can find new ones. Unemployment rises despite the productivity gains.

The third scenario assumes AI investments fail to deliver the returns Wall Street expects. Companies spend heavily on infrastructure, stock prices rise on expectations of huge profits, and those expectations eventually prove too optimistic.

“Equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown,” Warsh said. In that scenario, unemployment rises more sharply, and the economy eventually recovers without the promised productivity boost.

Those risks are already receiving attention elsewhere at the Fed. Governor Michael Barr warned Monday that the AI construction boom is increasingly financed through complex arrangements, including long-term computing leases, energy contracts and financial guarantees.

The Fed estimates that the potential maximum value of these off-balance-sheet obligations now exceeds $3 trillion. Those commitments are not the same as debt already owed, but they show why disappointing AI revenues could create problems beyond the technology companies building data centers.

Warsh did not propose an interest-rate change in Monday's remarks. The Fed's next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8 and 9.

#4926. HKMA, Swift explore tokenized deposits for cross-border bank payments

HKMA and Swift will explore linking Project Ensemble with Swift’s ledger for cross-border payments using tokenized deposits in multiple currencies.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Swift will explore connecting their payment infrastructure to support cross-border transfers using tokenized bank deposits, the authority said Monday.

The work will examine links between Swift’s blockchain-based ledger and the settlement infrastructure of Project Ensemble. Participating banks include Bank of China (Hong Kong), Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong) and HSBC, according to the announcement.

Tokenized deposits are bank balances represented on a blockchain. They remain claims on the issuing commercial bank, unlike central bank digital currencies, which are claims on a central bank. The proposed Swift connection would explore how separate payment systems could work together across borders in multiple currencies.

The collaboration follows a Nov. 2 upgrade to EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, enabling banks to settle tokenized deposit transactions around the clock using tokenized central bank money. The pilot launched in November 2025 and initially relied on Hong Kong’s dollar-denominated real-time gross settlement system.

In July, Swift said its blockchain-based ledger was ready for initial use and that it was preparing to pilot tokenized cross-border payments with 17 major banks, including Citi, DBS and HSBC.

One of our favorite details is the padding. “It’s built in—so you never have to deal with shifting, scrunching, or fishing pads out of the laundry,” Andriakos says. That means the bra keeps its shape wash after wash and eliminates the annoyance of removable inserts. The padding also stays comfortable through body changes—Andriakos says it even supported her during pregnancy and postpartum. The only potential downside is that the padding isn’t removable, which might not appeal to those who want less coverage.

The wide adjustable straps are another favorite feature of mine. They distribute weight evenly across my shoulders without digging in or creating pressure points during longer workouts. Even better, the straps adjust from the front, so it’s way easier to adjust than traditional bras.

And for my sweaty gals, the fabric is perfect for keeping perspiration under control. It’s made from a breathable, sweat-wicking blend of recycled polyester and elastane, which feels soft and flexible while maintaining shape. It also gives the bra a streamlined silhouette that sits smoothly under all my workout tops.

The Power+ is made from a compressive blend of polyester, nylon, and spandex and features multiple tension fabrics with strategically placed, double-layered support panels throughout the back and shoulders. Together, they create a gentle pull that encourages your shoulders to stay back and your chest open. Despite its posture-focused design, the Power+ also functions as a solid sports bra. Another unexpected perk: It’s just as helpful during everyday wear as it is in the gym. Compression, which can be found in the Nike or Lululemon sports bras, offers the feeling of your boobs being so supported that they’re a bit squished and pushed down. Encapsulation lifts, cradles, and separates your girls while still eliminating boob bounce. It can be found in the Beyond Yoga bra. #4923. Cancer Taught Dolph Lundgren He’s Not Invincible. Now He’s Finding New Strength.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

After three years with no evidence of disease, the action legend is training smarter—and living differently.

DOLPH LUNDGREN HAS had one hell of a life. From being plucked from obscurity into a modeling career after studying chemical engineering at MIT, to dating Grace Jones, to becoming one of the iconic bad guys of the 1980s, what hasn’t he done? Just one of those things would be a highlight in anybody’s life. But Dolph Lundgren isn’t just anybody.

Seemingly cut from stone and delivered to America ready-made to star in films, his path upon arrival from Sweden wasn’t always easy. In the new documentary, Dolph: Unbreakable, Lundgren gets candid about a childhood of abuse and the struggle to put that behind him. He also discusses the films he felt didn’t meet his standards after he was established as a household name thanks to roles in Rocky IV, Universal Soldier, and Masters of the Universe. While there are certainly gems to be discovered in that direct-to-video period, it's fascinating to watch the man many know as Ivan Drago, a brute with few words, open up about his life and career. Perhaps the film’s biggest revelation is that of Lundgren’s fight with cancer, a diagnosis that, at one point, gave him just a few months to live.

That fight scaffolds Dolph: Unbreakable, and it’s moving to watch a man so seemingly superhuman allow himself to be so vulnerable. Now, on the other side of that battle and going strong, Lundgren is out in the world touring with his new memoir, Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle, alongside the doc. Taking a moment from his busy schedule, the 69-year-old legend sat down with Men’s Health to discuss his new fitness app, Brandon Lee and learning from Sylvester Stallone.

MEN’S HEALTH: How’s your health these days?

DOLPH LUNDGREN: It's good, man. It's good. I've been NED—no evidence of disease—for three years now. I'm doing a scan every couple of months. I mean, I still work out. I work out a lot now, actually, like I used to. I’m feeling great. I'm working on a fitness app—My friend Arnold has one. I'm going to do a much smaller personal one about exactly how I work out; It's more confined to what I do.

But physically, I feel good. Psychologically, once you have the cancer diagnosis, you're always wondering what's going to come in the future, but it keeps you honest on some level. It keeps me honest about enjoying the moments.

MH: Even in the scariest moments of your diagnosis in the documentary, you always looked like you were in great shape. How has your approach to fitness evolved as you’ve gotten older?

DL: It's gotten a little more focused. As you get older, you have more responsibilities and you have less time, especially these days with all the digital noise in the world. I think I’ve also gotten a little smarter. The cancer journey made me realize I'm not invincible, and even though I want to do crazy stuff like I used to and spar with 25-year-olds and run up the mountain, I can’t do that anymore.

I said, "No, I'm going to cut back on the crazy stuff." And I've devised this workout schedule that's based on 30- to 40-minute workouts a couple times a week, and I've distilled it down to what I think really works, what doesn't get you injured, and what you have access to. Most people have access to a gym. So, most of it is strength training. There's some cardio involved, plus a little movement and mobility from martial arts. I've come up with a pretty clever and pretty efficient program.

MH: I love how candid you get in the film, especially about your own work. You’re hard on some of your direct-to-video work, but those projects still have a lot of fans. Is there anything you think went under the radar?

DL: Look, what I would say is I'm proud of my own work, but I may not be totally ecstatic about how the films turned out sometimes. I wasn't the director. Some of the movies, however, like Command Performance, I'm very proud of. That's a movie I directed. I think what I said in the doc was that the focus wasn’t necessarily to make a good movie. It was just to make quick money. I definitely feel good about the movies I directed. I feel good about Command Performance and Wanted Man. Movies like I Come in Peace—I know a lot of people like that one. Unfortunately, we couldn’t include that one in the documentary. There’s only so much space. [Laughs] They're all testaments of their time. They may not be prominent, but they've clearly played a part in my life and my development as a person and as an actor.

MH: Showdown in Little Tokyo is an all-time favorite of mine. I love your dynamic in it with Brandon Lee. What are your memories of him?

DL: My main memory of him is that he was a great guy. We really got along very well, both off-screen and on-screen. Obviously, I was a fan of his dad's, Bruce. I think his mom, Linda Lee, was half Swedish. I think her grandmother was from Sweden. He had been to Sweden, and had a quarter of Scandinavian descent. That's why he was tall, and had those good looks—that mix between her and Bruce.

He spoke some Swedish, and we bonded over that. Then, of course, the martial arts: he did the same style as his dad, and I was doing Kyokushin karate, a different style. We had such a great time together. I was very, very upset when I got that call a couple years later that he'd gotten killed in some freak accident. He would've certainly been a huge star.

MH: You were speaking earlier about your development as an actor. You’ve always been a compelling screen presence, but you’ve become better and better as you’ve gotten older. You give incredible performances in movies like Creed II and Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning. What’s it been like to stretch yourself?

DL: It's been great. I remember an interview with Russell Crowe where he was asked, "How do you create a great character?" And he says, "Work with a great director." It's hard to display great acting if you're not working with a great director, because he's the artist. That's why Marlon Brando made bad movies once in a while. He was usually interesting, but maybe the movie was forgettable.

As a martial artist, as an engineer, I was used to being trained from the ground up properly for years. Martial arts took seven years to get a black belt. I started acting when I was 23, and I was thrown into a big movie very quickly. The movie was a hit, and suddenly I'm in Hollywood. I'm now starring in my own movies, but I didn't have much experience. I had to learn on the job, and it wasn't easy. But think about Stallone, for instance. He’d done some great acting, but before that, he was a writer. He wanted to be a star early on. I hadn't even thought of it before Rocky IV. It took me years after that to acquire more confidence and skill.

With recent films, especially Creed II and Aquaman, I had a chance to work with better directors and actors, and play more interesting characters. I still do action stuff and action comedies where it's not as focused, but I do like to apply myself. Now, I'm interested in applying myself, post-cancer, to dramatic roles to see what happens, because I haven't done it yet. It's going to be interesting. I'm doing some of those kinds of movies this year and next year.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4922. Binance Pay Later offers credit backed by Bitcoin, Ether and BNB holdings

Eligible users can access up to 1,000 USDC in credit against their Bitcoin, Ether or BNB for purchases via Binance Card or QR Pay.

Binance said Monday it would offer eligible users in Argentina and Mexico up to 1,000 USDC in spending credit through Pay Later, a payment feature backed by their cryptocurrency holdings.

Pay Later allows eligible users to access up to 1,000 USDC (USDC) in spending power against their Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and BNB (BNB) token holdings as collateral, without selling the underlying assets, Binance said in an announcement shared with Cointelegraph. Borrowing is limited to 50% of the eligible collateral’s value, meaning $2,000 in BTC is required to access a maximum $1,000 credit line.

Purchases are interest-free until the repayment deadline on the first of the following month. Binance’s published FAQ lists a one-day grace period and interest of 0.1% per day, compounding daily, on overdue balances.

Borrowing lets users make purchases without first selling their crypto, but falling prices can put those holdings at risk. Binance can liquidate collateral when the outstanding loan reaches 90% of its value, even before repayment is due. It will initially launch for users in Argentina and Mexico, with a gradual rollout planned for additional markets.

“Traditional consumer credit often relies on income documentation and credit history, which leaves people who hold assets but have no formal credit file with fewer options,” said Thomas Gregory, VP of payments and fiat at Binance, adding that asset-backed credit offers an alternative.

#4921. Trump Backs Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia as Sam Altman Says 'Heroes Have Flaws'

Trump Backs Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia as Sam Altman Says 'Heroes Have Flaws'

President Donald Trump joined Elon Musk on Monday in supporting Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, while OpenAI chief Sam Altman expressed empathy for the ousted co-founder without endorsing his reinstatement.

“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters Monday as he left the White House for Asia, according to Reuters. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”

Trump said Huang had “learned a big lesson,” and questioned claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” he said, per The Guardian.

Trump also dismissed concerns that his ties with Huang threatened national security and defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick amid questions over enforcement of AI-chip export controls.

Musk also said Friday he was signing a petition demanding Huang’s reinstatement.

“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk wrote on X. Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad are also listed among the supporters.

More than 182,000 people had signed the open letter by Monday. It seeks Huang’s return during an independent investigation, although signatories’ identities and affiliations are not independently verified.

Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference Monday, Altman said Huang had “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” He described feeling “personal strong empathy” for the former Nvidia boss.

He has reason to understand a boardroom revolt. OpenAI fired Altman in November 2023, only to reinstate him less than five days later after employee and investor backlash. Still, asked whether Huang should return, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

Altman said he struggled to imagine Nvidia without Huang, but argued the giant chipmaker was big enough to retain investor trust. That is sympathy—not an endorsement.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, stepped down Thursday after admitting infidelity. Reports later linked him to Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees, one a subordinate.

Alice Huang previously worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer facing scrutiny over possible diversion of advanced chips to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing; espionage allegations remain unproven.

Washington is tightening export controls on advanced AI chips, including new licensing requirements for shipments to Singapore and Malaysia, as officials seek to prevent diversion to China.

Trump’s backing also puts him at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said Sunday that Nvidia should look outside its ranks for a replacement. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent told Fox News.

Nvidia’s board has made no decision to reinstate Huang. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, while the Financial Times reports Huang’s allies are lobbying for his return and Arm CEO Rene Haas is a potential successor.

Employees have also pushed for reinstatement. An internal discussion drew more than 1,600 comments, including calls for Huang’s return.

Nvidia shares opened 2.7% lower Monday, wiping out roughly $100 billion in market value at the open.

Huang could face congressional questions on China chip exports in early December. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, its first financial update under Kress.

#4920. Strategy buys $33M in Bitcoin, spends $228M on STRC buybacks

Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million and spent $228.1 million repurchasing STRC preferred shares, largely funded by new common stock sales.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million last week while spending nearly seven times as much repurchasing STRC preferred shares.

The company purchased the Bitcoin (BTC) at an average price of $68,887 between Monday and Sunday, bringing its holdings to 850,849 BTC, according to a Monday filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

Strategy said it raised $244.7 million by selling 2.09 million common shares (MSTR), using $33.4 million to buy Bitcoin, $206.3 million to fund STRC repurchases and $5 million to its separate cash balance. It funded the remaining $21.8 million in buybacks with interest earned on its cash and short-term investments.

The company repurchased 2.28 million STRC shares during the week. STRC is Strategy’s variable-rate preferred stock, which pays regular dividends to shareholders.

Strategy reported a $4.75 billion US dollar reserve after using $18.9 million to pay preferred stock dividends. Its separate cash balance stood at $151.2 million as of Sunday.

The company also maintained STRC’s annual dividend rate at 12% for December, saying it intends to keep the rate steady until the shares demonstrate sustained trading near $100.

Strategy spent $188.3 million repurchasing STRC shares and $81.9 million buying Bitcoin the previous week.

Strategy’s MSTR stock fell 8.45% to $102.2 in Monday’s premarket trading, while STRC declined 0.78% to $99.1, according to Yahoo Finance. The losses followed MSCI’s confirmation last week that it would remove Strategy from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close.

#4919. The 10 Most Comfortable Bras, According to Style Editors

I’ve tested more bras than I can count as a style writer. And over the years, I’ve learned that comfort is a nonnegotiable—if it digs, pinches, or rides up, it doesn’t deserve a space in my drawer. The thing is, no two boobs are exactly alike (not even your own). One might sit higher, be fuller, or have a different shape than the other. So finding the right bra isn’t about hitting a standard size—it’s about understanding your body. According to Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician and Women’s Health advisor, the right bra boosts comfort, improves posture, and eases back pain by evenly distributing breast tissue. If your band rides up, your straps slide, or your underwire doesn’t lie flat, it’s a clear sign something’s off.

And if your usual size suddenly stops working? Totally normal. Bra fitter and undergarment educator Kimmay Caldwell says weight changes, hormone shifts, or your monthly cycle can impact your size. To make it trickier, some brands still use outdated sizing methods (like the “plus four” rule), while others go by your exact underbust. Bottom line: your size can change and vary between clothing brands.

All of that can make bra shopping feel like a bit of a minefield, which is exactly why I tested 20 different styles across fits, fabrics, and support levels to find the ones that are actually worth your money. These ten passed the wear test and then some, proving that comfort, support, and style actually can exist in one bra.

A bra should fit your body—not the other way around—and Knix totally got the memo with this one. It feels snug at first, but it softens and molds to your shape with every wear. What really impressed me was the fit because it almost feels custom, thanks to the ultra-thin foam that contours without adding volume.

Plus, the sleek fabric (a nylon-spandex blend) moves with you, feeling super smooth against the skin and breathable enough to wear for hours.

If you're after definition without the discomfort, this wire-free option def delivers. The molded cups lift and separate, while subtle side padding helps prevent spillage and sideboob. The result? A natural shape, no extra bulk, and no awkward lines under tighter tops. And with 99 sizes (!!) and eight colors, the options are actually inclusive.

The only downside? It’s not the best for high movement and workouts. I find myself adjusting it when I bend or move quickly. Still, for everyday comfort and a super flattering fit, this one’s a standout.

The lightly contoured foam cups provide just enough structure to prevent the dreaded uniboob, while the wide, stretchy band stays comfortably in place without pinching or rolling. The smooth, buttery fabric feels soft against the skin and disappears nicely under T-shirts and other fitted tops.

It lifts and shapes without feeling restrictive, and the wider straps help distribute weight so your shoulders don't pay the price after hours of wear. Push-up bras with underwires have a bad rep, and for good reason. They’re usually stiff, pokey, and downright uncomfortable. But after wearing this Maidenform bra for months (yes, months), I can confidently say it’s a major exception to the rule.

The triangle shape gives a natural lift—no wires, no padding, just your boobs but sliiightly perkier.

Comfort-wise, it lives up to the name. The modal fabric is buttery-soft and stretchy in that live-in-it kind of way. The band is wide and smooth, so it stays put without digging, and the adjustable straps let you customize the fit. It’s also lightweight enough to forget you’re even wearing it.

It’s become my go-to for daily wear, and the super-soft, barely-there material is truly the next best thing to going bra-free. While it’s equally great for bed-rotting or taking Zoom calls from home, I also feel confident wearing it out and about because it doesn’t skimp on coverage and offers just enough support.

Even without padding, the double-layered fabric gives solid nipple coverage. It comes in inclusive sizes and neutral shades that go with everything. The few cons? It’s not super supportive for heavy movement or fuller busts, so you may need to readjust on the go. But for everyday wear, especially with low-cut outfits, it fits the bill.

The most comfortable bras usually come down to the right blend of fabrics. Here’s what each one brings to the table:

Comfort is about more than just size—it’s also about ensuring the wire doesn’t create pressure points or cause discomfort throughout the day. Look for bras with flexible, padded, or cushioned underwires, which offer support without digging into your skin. The underwire should sit flat against your ribcage and follow the natural curve of your breasts. If it feels like it’s poking or shifting, it’s not the right fit. If you prefer a wire-free bra, opt for styles with flexible boning, molded cups, and wide, flexible bands to provide support.

The most accurate way to find your size is to get fitted in person. Once you have your size, your new bra should feel snug and secure. The band should be comfortably tight, but not dig into the skin. A good rule of thumb is that you should be able to fit two fingers between the band and your skin, but no more. The cups should also lie flat against your chest.

The Women’s Health team has been testing bras since we first wrote this story in 2023. To find the most comfortable options, our team wore each style for at least a few weeks at a time. We wore them under different circumstances, including workouts, lounging, and long days at the office. But our main criterion for each bra was comfort. I also spoke with two bra experts and personally tested 20-plus bras over several years to lock down the ones I actually wear on repeat.

I recently re-tested a bunch of options and tapped style contributor Lily Wohlner for an update to this story to boost our list and keep it up-to-date. The final guide includes everything from bralettes and seamless bras to push-up bras—and I actually wear all of them in my day-to-day life.

#4918. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4917. Banks are banning AI agents over security... and competition concerns

AI agents are set to automate everyday banking tasks — but banks aren’t ready to give up control of the customer relationship just yet.

Banks in the United Kingdom have drawn a line over how much access artificial intelligence should have to their customers’ money.

Four banks, including HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest and Nationwide, have all moved to block or restrict third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, especially where they can make transactions without customer involvement.

There’s no evidence yet of AI agents accessing UK bank accounts just yet, but large lenders are worried about what happens if an automated system mismanages customers’ money — and who would be on the hook.

The banks might have other, unspoken concerns too.

Edgars Nemše, chief executive of GenLayer Foundation, an AI-focused blockchain infrastructure project, says routine banking tasks like paying bills, moving money and finding better rates could all be handed to agents.

Unfortunately for banks, this means agents would be able to seamlessly find customers a better deal elsewhere as soon as it’s published on the web.

“For plain accounts, that removes the switching costs and makes the space even more competitive,” Nemše tells Magazine.

That scenario could threaten more than just customer loyalty. In September, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok warned about a possible “agentic bank run.”

If swarms of agents start moving household cash from low-yield checking accounts to alternatives offering higher returns en masse, that would drain banks of the low-cost funding they rely on to make loans. And the speed and scale “would be a problem for the entire financial system.”

Related: Coinbase CEO touts agentic finance as Base tops 100M AI payments

JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon has also warned against allowing external agents unrestricted access to bank accounts. “You don’t want rogue agents,” he said on an October earnings call.

Is an agentic bank run coming? Source: Apollo

Regardless of short-term moves to hold back the tide, AI agents look more and more likely to revolutionize banking within a few years.

Neeraj Makin, group head of strategy analytics at Emirates NBD, predicts agents will usher in a new era of around-the-clock banking and near-instant payments as normal by 2036.

“Forget about waiting for a payment for 24 hours or inter-country payments taking three days… all of that will be in seconds, atomic,” he says, with AI agents taking over most financial decisions.

Ferdinand Dabitz, chief executive of Augustus, an AI-native banking and payments company, sees a similar shift in how customers interact with financial institutions.

“Every consumer will have 10s and every business will have 100s of agents talking to their bank,” Dabitz says.

A human interface will still remain important for managing those agents and providing a layer of trust, “especially in commercial banking,” he says.

Related: Agents can trade 24/7 — but Yat Siu warns you could lose access at any time

Emirates NBD’s developer experience team argued in July that financial institutions should build their own frameworks for agentic AI, rather than allowing individual teams to develop agents without common controls.

Its Leap framework is designed to govern how agents authenticate with core banking systems, access sensitive data and carry out actions, with audit trails, monitoring and human oversight built in.

Emirates NBD says banks should build their own agentic frameworks. Source: Emirates NBD

However there are still major concerns around the reliability of agents to make major financial decisions on their own.

A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found that while 80% of responding firms had deployed AI agents, just 2% used agents with broad autonomy, identifying data security, third-party dependencies and risks like hallucinations among their biggest concerns.

The AI takeover likely won’t happen overnight; “it will come in steps,” Nemše says.

“Today I use an agent to review my own and my company’s finances every month and queue the payments, and I approve them. The next step is the natural one: once you trust it, you let it spend small amounts without asking.”

Routine bills, subscriptions and the agent’s own running costs would be among the first tasks to become autonomous, he says.

Dabitz says corporate treasury management could be an area delegated to agents, but says banks will need to be involved in developing these early applications.

While consumers may enjoy the upside of automating their finances, who’s on the hook when an agent makes a mistake?

Nemše says banks need to offer “delegated access as a normal feature” to avoid customers sharing logins with agents. Customers could set permissions and spending limits, and agents could make low-value transactions independently while requiring approval for larger amounts.

But existing dispute processes may struggle if agents begin making thousands of transactions on behalf of each customer. “Even a small share going wrong is a lot of disputes,” he says. “The processes for handling them were built for people making a few payments a week. That part still has to be built.”

The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a supervisory framework for banks’ use of what it calls “super intelligence,” including agentic systems, on Nov. 4.

OCC’s Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework. Source: OCC

The framework is meant to help bank examiners assess how institutions use the technology, and does not introduce new binding requirements for banks. Scrutiny should reflect the potential consequences of an agent’s actions, its level of autonomy and the degree of human oversight.

So an AI system helping a bank employee draft a report would present a different risk from one authorized to move customer funds without approval, and the banks that get that balance right are likely to come out on top.

#4916. Clarity Act Defeat ‘Failure of American Leadership’: Trump’s Former Crypto Chief

Clarity Act Defeat ‘Failure of American Leadership’: Trump’s Former Crypto Chief

The Senate's failure to pass the Clarity Act was "a failure of American leadership," according to Patrick Witt, President Donald Trump's former top crypto adviser.

"It was extremely disappointing," Witt said in an on-stage interview at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London. "I was knee deep in Clarity. I lived it for a year plus negotiating that bill," he noted, adding that the bill, "would have been incredibly impactful."

Witt served as executive director of the President's Council of Advisers for Digital Assets until last month and led the White House push for the bill, which would have set out a framework for regulating crypto markets. It failed a key procedural vote in the Senate in September.

"We ultimately lost against the clock," he said, adding that, "The policy was good. We resolved pretty much all of the policy differences." But with the midterm elections approaching, "the political issue of ethics really consumed everything else," he said.

Democrats had raised concerns over the Trump family's crypto ventures. Witt acknowledged that Trump's involvement in crypto was "arguably the issue," but said the president had agreed to two ethics provisions. The second would have barred federal officials, including the president, from issuing or sponsoring digital assets, forced the president to divest certain digital assets or put them in a blind trust, and let state attorneys general enforce violations. "There's no precedent for those kinds of things in American law," he said.

The GENIUS stablecoin bill also lost an initial procedural vote in 2025 but recovered because it came early in Trump's term, Witt noted. With Clarity, "we knew that we were going to get one shot at it, and unfortunately we just came up short," he said.

Looking ahead, Witt said the odds of passing a comprehensive replacement are low. "I would expect that market structure in the United States is going to be less written on Capitol Hill and more written in the Federal Register, which is where the agencies do their rulemakings and issue their guidance," Witt said.

Parts of the Clarity Act could still pass in larger legislative packages, and lawmakers could grant targeted powers, such as giving the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over spot crypto markets, he said.

Witt said regulators already have "ample authority," and that the administration had to "hold them back a little bit" while the bill played out. The SEC and CFTC have since moved ahead with their own crypto rules, though House Financial Services Committee Chairman French Hill (R-AR) has said those efforts fall short of what the legislation would have achieved.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins and CFTC Chair Michael Selig "are committed to moving markets on chain," Witt said, framing the issue as one of American competitiveness. "Capital is going to go where it's treated best," he said.

Despite Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterms, Witt said he is "not bearish on the industry overall," since the regulators and the president remain in place. Democrats are reportedly planning to push their own, broader market structure bill.

He said opposition to crypto is increasingly generational rather than purely partisan. While some Democrats, such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), are "going to be 100% opposed to anything that seemingly is favorable to crypto," younger lawmakers on both sides see it as "part of the fabric of financial infrastructure," he said, pointing to Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) and Ruben Gallego (D-AZ).

Witt left the administration in October, The Hill reported. He said he has held talks with crypto firms, venture capital firms and defense companies, and hopes to announce his next move in the coming weeks.

#4915. The 10 Best Workout Tops for Women of 2026, Tested by Experts and Editors

Our fave option on this list is from Beyond Yoga.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve spent years logging miles, reps, and classes in all types of activewear; which means I’ve tested more workout tops than I can count. From Pilates to outdoor runs to heavy lifting sessions, I know exactly what separates a top you forget you’re wearing from one you can’t wait to peel off. For me, the best workout tops for women nail comfort, offer just enough support, and look flattering.

The last thing you want is an overly tight top that clips your movement (especially during yoga!), but it should still provide enough compression to hold you and the girls in, says Rebecca Stewart, CPT, a trainer and mobility coach. While you could make do with a regular cotton t-shirt during your workout sesh, it won't offer the same level of support, mobility, or sweat-wicking capabilities.

Finding the right workout top all comes down to personal preference. Because there are so many options to choose from—think T-shirts, tanks, and long-sleeve tops—we asked experts and tested tons of options ourselves to find styles we think will fit a wide range of needs and preferences. From lightweight, flowy options to compression shirts great for high-intensity workouts, our absolute favorite workout tops below are highlighted below.

Over the last few months I’ve tested a handful of workout tops and the Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Cropped Tank topped my list for a few reasons: It’s super comfortable (it won a spot for the softest bra in our Best Racerback Bras story!), has a built-in shelf bra, is size inclusive, and comes in a ton of vibrant and neutral shades.

It's basically the two-in-one bra and workout tank combo you didn’t know you needed. Made from the brand’s signature polyester and elastane blend, it’s the comfiest and most lightweight option I’ve ever worn. It feels like you're wearing nothing at all, but it still keeps the girls in place with a medium-level compression that’s perfect for light to moderate workouts. The cherry on top? It’s moisture-wicking, so it keeps you dry whether you’re working out or just running around on a hot day.

Our only gripe: If you have a bigger chest, you’ll probably want to layer a sports bra underneath for extra support. But if you're part of the itty bitty titty committee, you're good to go wearing this solo pretty much anywhere.

Read More: Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Tank Review

ICYMI, Amazon Essentials Activewear is where it’s at for affordable workout basics that rival the quality of some of the more luxe brands we’ve tried. The cotton, modal, and elastane blend feels thick, substantial, and smooth to the touch. It’s the kind of material that holds up well throughout repeated workouts and wash cycles, so you can keep this workout tee in constant rotation.

We also love the subtle crop length that isn’t too short or too long. It gives you room to move without showing too much skin, and has a semi-relaxed fit that perfectly skims the body. It’s extremely soft, but thanks to the touch of elastane in the fabric, it has ample stretch so you don’t feel constricted during overhead lifts or higher-impact workouts like running or HIIT.

The only con is that the white color can be slightly see-through. We suggest opting for a darker shade or wearing a flesh-toned bra underneath. The color options are also a little limited, but we love the slate gray and light blue options.

WH editors have tried a lot of workout tops over the years and agree that the Lululemon Ebb to Street Tank is a reliable favorite. It’s super soft, seamless, sweat-wicking, and ultra stretchy thanks to a comfortable blend of elastane and nylon. Plus, it offers just the right amount of support and coverage for low-impact workouts like Pilates, yoga, and walking.

The most convenient part: it has a built-in shelf bra, so you don’t have to wear a separate bra underneath (unless you want to for more support!). And, we found that it actually does keep us feeling covered and protected during low-impact exercise, which we didn’t find to be the case with other tanks that have built-in bras. Another pro? The longer length of this top (it hits at the hip) keeps us feeling locked in and covered during workouts where we don’t want a ton of stomach showing.

“I love how versatile this top is, along with its longer length and the buttery-soft blend of nylon and elastane,” says trainer Kristina Earnest, CPT, founder of Kristina Earnest On Demand. This is her go-to top when she's working out at home, and she wears it under a sweater for her cold weather errands. It feels incredibly comfortable thanks to its seamless racerback design—no pesky straps, seams, or tightness to get in the way during your sweat session. However, you should note that because there are no adjustable straps, you can't customize the fit of this tank.We put this tank to the test during a variety of workouts, like HIIT training and running, and found that it’s not the best choice for high-intensity training. We noticed that it didn’t do a great job of holding the breasts in place during high-impact moves and felt the need for more padding and compression. But based on our extensive testing, it's difficult to find a tank with high-impact support. That's why we recommend pairing this with our favorite high-impact sports bra, the Under Armour Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra.

This tank is meant to be worn over your favorite sports bra as an added layer of coverage. The loose, cropped fit is easy to throw on, and the round neck with the knotted side detail adds a touch of style. Our fave part about this tank? The cotton material is super breathable, so you never feel overheated or constricted like you would with a tighter top.

“I love that this top isn’t too tight,” says Jacqueline Kasen, CPT, trainer and senior director of group fitness at Anatomy. “It’s super comfortable and loose whether you’re running or lifting, but it still stays in place without bunching up.” Plus, it holds its shape after multiple washes and never pills or frays, making it as durable as it is functional.

The tank is made with cotton, but it also has a bit of spandex woven throughout, which makes it stretchy and not too sturdy. This is essential during workouts, as you want your top to move with you instead of against you at the gym.

We noticed that the shirt can look a bit boxy if you go too oversized, so we recommend sizing down for a more flattering, snug fit.

This short-sleeve workout top from Under Armour is a game changer for high-intensity exercise since it offers both compression and cooling technology. It’s designed as a baselayer to keep you protected under your sports gear (by preventing pinching and chafing), but we love to wear it on its own as a temperature-regulating, sweat-wicking, ultra-lightweight workout top.

This t-shirt has an ultra-tight, compressive fit (which can help with circulation and muscular endurance), but it is super thin and made with the brand's HeatGear fabric to keep you from overheating. It’s made from polyester for a smooth, lightweight feel, plus elastane for a generous amount of stretch. We love that this top is breathable and moisture-wicking, so even though it’s on the tighter side, it doesn’t feel like you’re wearing anything. Whether you’re lifting heavy or doing sprints outdoors, this top is perfect for keeping you cool, dry, and comfortable.

However, this top (like most compressive gear) might not be the best option for lower-impact exercise or workouts that require lots of stretching and bending—like yoga or Pilates. We generally opt for looser, softer fits for these workouts and stick to tighter tops for strength training and cardio.

Listen, I love a cute lil workout set as much as the next Pilates princess, but sometimes I don’t want to bare my entire midriff. That’s where an oversized workout top like this one comes in clutch. I especially love it in white because it's just a touch see-through, so it lets me show off my matching sports bra and workout short combo without feeling exposed. It’s also perfect for those days when I feel a little bloated and just need something loose-fitting that won’t emphasize my stomach.

Unlike the other workout tops you’ll find here, this tee is made from 100% cotton. The natural fiber is not exactly known for its high-performance abilities at the gym (it doesn’t wick sweat very well), but the thinner construction and super boxy fit help keep things super airy. I wore it for an outdoor workout over the summer and felt cool and comfortable—well, as much as you can while doing burpees.

It’s also just a really cute shape. I love the sleeves, which, despite being those of a t-shirt, hit at about the elbow, giving it a really laidback feel. I love it for working out or for throwing on over my skin-tight sets to and from Pilates, but I also find myself grabbing it day-to-day for errands and casual outings. I frequently throw it on over a bright tank styled with some longline biker shorts and comfy sneaks for a cool-girl fit that basically feels like I’m wearing pajamas.

As with any oversized workout tee, it might not be the wisest choice for HIIT workouts or anything super tactical. The billowing sleeves and loose fit could get caught on equipment or flop over your face while bending or jumping.

An open-back top is not only a super stylish choice, but it helps keep you cool as a cucumber during sweaty workouts too. I especially love this top for hot Pilates when I want as little fabric against my skin as possible. And since it has built-in padding (that doesn’t shift around in the wash!), I can literally just wear this on its own to yoga, Pilates, strength training, or other low-impact workouts.

I have worn this during my more intense exercise like an Orangetheory class or while running, and it does offer enough support for me (as someone who teeters between a C cup and a D cup). But if you have a larger chest size, it might be best to reserve this top for low-impact movement or layer it over your favorite sports bra.

Nike’s Dri-FIT tech (a blend of nylon and spandex) is also a major pro. It feels sleek and smooth against the skin but also helps move sweat away from the body. When I leave an intense workout class (even a heated one), it’s noticeable how much less sweat I have sitting between my skin and my workout top when I reach for this one, which is huge for me, since I’ve been struggling with eczema that gets worse with heat and sweat.

The material is also suuuper stretchy and comfortable, and never gets in the way of any kind of movement, whether that’s mat Pilates or an intense upper-body session at the gym. It’s also really lightweight so it feels nearly like a second skin and never requires adjustments mid-workout.

This tank from Gymshark pairs perfectly with the brand’s bestselling leggings. Like the leggings, this tank is nearly seamless—the only seams are along the bottom hem, but they are super flat and don’t cause any rubbing or chafing when up against the skin.

I love that the stretchy, smooth fabric (made of 96% nylon and 4% elastane) is basically sweat-proof and dries super quickly. That’s because nylon is a synthetic fabric that’s hydrophobic (i.e. it resists the penetration of water), so this top is great for wicking moisture away from the body during intense workouts.

Not only that, but it’s super cute, too. I love the square neckline and the length that hits right at the hip bones. It also has a built-in shelf bra to help support and lift the girls for a more flattering shape and a little extra protection against bounce during your workouts. It might not be enough support for larger chest sizes during high-intensity movement, but for smaller chests and moderate activity, it does the trick.

We’ve all been in those super stuffy gyms. When I start overheating during a workout, all I want is to be in a sports bra. But I’m not always comfortable showing my stomach. That’s where the Wild Thing Bra comes in. With its longline fit, which ends just above my belly button for slightly more coverage than a standard sports bra, the top leaves me feeling cool and comfortable at the gym.

And, of course, it’s super cute, thanks to the ruching in the center of the bra. I find this detail really flattering—it gives my stomach a snatched look when I wear it. While it doesn’t offer a ton of support since it’s on the lighter side, it provides decent compression for my higher intensity workouts. Its lightweight design and stylish details make it perfect for pairing with leggings at the gym, but I’ve also seen it styled with trousers or jeans for a sporty yet upscale vibe.

Worried about the lighter colors looking sheer? Don’t be! All styles come with removable cups to cover your girls, which is also helpful because you can take them out when you wash the bra. Speaking of washing, we find that this bra holds up well after multiple washes and never pills or changes in elasticity and shape.

One thing to keep in mind is that the straps aren’t adjustable, which can be a bit frustrating since it means you can’t customize the fit. I also wish it came in more colors.

This tank won the top spot in our Best Workout Tank Tops story for a few reasons: It's super flattering, never rides up, is compressive, supportive, and sweat-wicking.

We tested this ribbed tank across many different workouts—running, yoga, lifting, and HIIT—and we found that it never moves or rides up. And, we love that it’s a tighter spandex tank with high compression, as it holds us in all the right places and doesn’t allow for any boob bounce. It doesn’t have a built-in bra, but it’s tight enough to hold the chest in place.

It's also super moisture-wicking. WH assistant fashion editor Rose Lauture wore this during an intense workout and said there were no sweat stains, no matter which color she wore, thanks to the soft nylon. Because it's moisture-wicking, it also does a great job at preventing body odor.

This option offers some pretty solid support for not having a built-in bra (it's all about the compression!). However, it is made for medium support, so we like to wear an extra bra underneath this tank from time to time when our workouts get extra intense.

Stewart’s pro tip? For high-impact or high-intensity workouts, look for materials that are shiny and smooth to reduce chafing and wick sweat. For lower-intensity workouts, look for matte fabrics that have a soft, buttery texture for comfort and flexibility.

Should your workout top be loose or tight? While it does come down to personal preference, there are pros and cons to each. Tighter tops don’t get in the way of movement as much as a looser top might: they often feel more secure and supportive. But if you find looser tops more comfortable, they can certainly work for nearly every workout except for those involving a Pilates reformer (where loose fabric can easily get caught) or other equipment like cable machines.

Some workout tops have built-in shelf bras or bra pad inserts, but this can be a “love it or hate it” situation, says Stewart. For bigger busts or high-intensity activities, a built-in bra may not provide enough support, so you might need an extra sports bra underneath. However, for smaller busts, we find that they provide ample support for light- and medium-intensity workouts. “A built-in bra should feel supportive and not bothersome and shouldn’t be too tight or digging in to restrict your movement,” says Stewart.

There are tons of workout tops out there, so even finding the absolute best options to test was difficult. When I began the November 2026 update of this article, I revisited our original February 2024 story to see which of the picks our team is still wearing. Some of them are still team favorites, but I went back to the drawing board and asked fitness experts and stylists, including style contributors Kristen Saladino, Rose Lauture, and Lily Wohlner, which workout tops they were loving. From there, I removed the picks that we are no longer wearing and added the options we’ve been reaching for the most.

I made sure that the final picks on this list were options that we wear across all sorts of activities, from compressive options perfect for HIIT workout classes to lightweight, flowy tops we like for lounging or lower-impact exercise. Some of the contenders on this list come in tons of different colors and styles, have built-in bras, and are made with the highest-quality materials for their price points.

#4913. Lighter recovers $5M after $10M exploit linked to compromised API keys

Lighter restored withdrawals after recovering approximately $5 million in USDC, while blockchain analysts traced $10.4 million in funds moved during the exploit.

Update 20:40 UTC: This article has been updated with details of Lighter’s $5 million fund recovery, the restoration of withdrawals and the cause of the exploit.

Decentralized derivatives exchange Lighter said it had restored withdrawals and recovered approximately $5 million after an attacker exploited compromised trader API keys in an incident involving more than $10 million in withdrawals Monday.

Blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps said about $10.4 million in USDC had been withdrawn from the platform. It tracked funds being swapped into Ether (ETH) and Wrapped Monero XMR1, a token traded on Hyperliquid.

Lighter initially said its protocol and smart contracts were unaffected. The exchange activated Guardian mode, temporarily pausing withdrawals and new pool creation while its Security Council worked to secure the platform.

The security incident follows a string of high-profile cryptocurrency exploits this year, including the $6.3 billion Binance hack on Oct. 29, the industry’s largest to date.

Lighter and Bubblemaps identified wallet ‘0xb3f’ as the attacker’s address. Blockchain data platform Bitquery separately traced 10,393,057 USDC leaving Lighter’s Ethereum contract at 10:11 am UTC. It said most of those funds were converted into Ether through CoW Swap within minutes, followed by a series of 160 ETH transfers to wallets linked to XMR1 purchases on Hyperliquid.

Related: DOJ moves to seize $1.2B from Binance hack, disrupts FaceStealer scam

In subsequent analysis, Bitquery identified a total of 1,920 ETH transferred through 12 wallets, each receiving 160 ETH (about $290,000) before routing the funds through LI.FI toward Hyperliquid.

The 12 Hyperliquid accounts purchased approximately $3.46 million in XMR1 tokens. Another 3,845 ETH, worth about $7 million, remained in the original wallet as of 11:55 UTC on Monday, according to Bitquery’s latest snapshot.

Bitquery also identified similar fund movements following a separate $6.45 million Safe wallet theft at 11:35 UTC on Monday, about 84 minutes after the Lighter withdrawal, as well as a Kava exploit two days earlier.

All three involved funds routed through LI.FI into XMR1 purchases on Hyperliquid, but Bitquery found no direct transfers linking either of the other incidents to Lighter. The firm cautioned that similar transaction routes alone are weak evidence of a common attacker.

In a postmortem published Monday at 18:20 UTC, Lighter detailed how the attacker obtained private API keys through a trader’s custom signing software, which reused cryptographic nonces, allowing the keys to be calculated from publicly available signatures.

The attacker used the compromised keys to create a public pool, transfer funds into it and withdraw them through an attacker-controlled account.

Lighter said its Guardian security mechanism temporarily paused withdrawals, allowing its Security Council to return approximately $5 million in USDC to the affected trader. The exchange said its protocol, smart contracts and official software development kits were unaffected.

Lighter has since required wallet signatures for transfers to public pools and made API-key signatures non-public. It also plans to introduce IP allowlists and configurable permissions for API keys.

#4912. 17 Best Airbnb Cabins for a Picture-Perfect Outdoor Retreat (2026)

Picture this: A wood-burning stove, a claw-foot tub, no cell service, and no news. Are you in heaven? Or are you in one of the best Airbnb cabins we’ve rounded up across the US? Whether it’s an organic design marvel in Washington that would make Frank Lloyd Wright weep or a sauna-equipped “bird house” cabin in Wisconsin that piques your interest, there are so many places to enjoy the great outdoors in style. So, if immaculate cabin rentals make up your fall and winter travel mood board, look to these cozy cabins, tiny homes, chalets, and comfortable cottages for a weekend getaway. Think: elevated A-frames and Lincoln log-style beauties, fleshed out with curated amenities and thoughtful design details. Here, you can get a little lost in the beauty of the wilderness (without giving up too much in the way of modern accommodations).

Perks: Indoor fireplace, private patio, barbecue grill, sound system, security system, free parking

A steeply pitched roof and black metal siding give this tiny cabin near Oregon’s Mount Hood a striking silhouette against the towering pines. Designed by a professional architect, the 190-square-foot retreat takes its cues from shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice of forest bathing. The exterior pairs dark metal with warm pine cladding, while oversized windows look out to picturesque woodland views. Inside, there's a sound system, queen bed, wood-burning stove, and compact kitchenette, but the real luxury is falling asleep to natural white noise from the surrounding forest. Even the shower comes with a forest view, making this a particularly appealing place to spend a weekend off the grid. From $381 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, forest views, private balcony, fireplace, fire pit, nearby hiking trails, nearby skiing, private security

At nearly 11,000 feet above sea level, this Breckenridge cabin puts you practically eye to eye with Colorado’s towering Quandary Peak. Getting there involves climbing about 60 steps through the evergreens, but the payoff is a private balcony with sweeping mountain views. Inside, the renovated retreat has a Scandinavian-inspired aesthetic, with warm wood finishes, cozy textiles, and a gas fireplace for snowy evenings. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, while outside, a firepit offers another spot to take in the alpine scenery. Downtown Breckenridge is just 15 minutes away, though between the mountain views and the deck, there’s plenty of incentive to stay put. From $365 per night.

Perks: Mountain view, wood-fired hot tub, indoor fireplace, fire pit, private backyard, hiking, free parking

The Blue Ridge Mountains are the main attraction at Doah House, a cabin perched high above Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. A 16-foot wall of sliding glass doors opens onto a wraparound deck, making the one-of-a-kind forest views visible from anywhere in the living room. Inside the blonde wood interiors, a wood-burning stove, heated floors, and a lofted bedroom equipped with a queen-sized bed add to the appeal. The bathroom features Moroccan tile, a rainfall shower, and a floor-to-ceiling window overlooking the trees. Outside, a private wood-fired hot tub and firepit make a strong case for spending the evening at the cabin, though Shenandoah National Park, Appalachian Trail hikes, and local wineries are all within reach. From $204 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, hot tub, sauna, fire pit, wood-burning stove, BBQ grill, heated bathroom floors free parking

Fresh eggs from the chicken coop, herbs picked straight from the garden, and a creekside sauna are just a few of the unexpected perks at Firelight at Shope Creek, a collection of eight cabins spread across 22 wooded acres outside Asheville, North Carolina. Cozy flourishes fill this 650-square-foot retreat with modern design, like a wood-burning stove, heated bathroom floors, and a spacious deck overlooking the surrounding mountains and meadows. There's also a private hot tub just steps from the king-size bedroom, ideally positioned for stargazing after dark. Guests can wander the property's private hiking trails, gather around the communal firepits, or settle into the covered outdoor pavilion, which has its own fireplace. And despite the secluded setting, downtown Asheville and the Blue Ridge Parkway are only about 20 minutes away. From $320 per night.

Perks: Hiking trails, swimming, hot tub, fire pit, sound system, fireplace, washer/dryer

During the day, a generous amount of sunlight pours into this secluded Maine cabin, illuminating thoughtful architectural details like floor-to-celing wood paneled walls and heightened ceilings. After sunset, a well-curated lighting scheme sets the mood, affording the opportunity to test-drive the property’s record player sound system and transform the main living area into a vinyl listening den. Don’t expect to spend all your time indoors, though. Outside of this modern cabin, there’s no shortage of adventures to explore, from swimming in the lake to hiking one of several nature trails close by. Boating rentals and the local golf course offer even more ways to spend your stay, as well as winter skiing or snowboarding just a 40-minute drive away. From $645 per night.

Perks: Ocean view, shared outdoor pool, sauna, fireplace, beach access

Private and serene, sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean surround this Sea Ranch cabin escape that meets the California coast. Best suited for a couples getaway or a duo vacation, an open floor plan and 30-foot-high ceilings ensure that the space doesn’t feel overly cramped, while oversized windows drench the rental in sunlight on cloudless days. Modern upgrades like minimalist furniture silhouettes, recognizable decor, and an updated kitchen bring contemporary flair to the home’s original timber frame built back in 1965. Outside, an expansive deck overlooking the nearby meadow is a natural place to enjoy morning coffee or your current novel. Walk along the bluff to one of several bordering beaches, or visit one of the private recreation centers to work on your tennis backhand or swimming skills indoors. From $681 per night.

Perks: Lake view, fireplace, BBQ grill, fire pit, free parking, washer/dryer

Tucked among the Wisconsin woodlands, MetalLark Tower is surrounded by impressive views, supplied by the nearby wildflower meadow and clandestine lake. The 800-square-foot home’s interiors are equally noteworthy, following modern Scandinavian design principles that make the space feel intentional and cozy. (Think: simple furniture silhouettes and a neutral color palette with light wood tones contrasted by stark black and grey accents). When you’re not admiring the dramatic floor-to-ceiling windows with stunning, 360-degree views of the region, the outdoor living area has lots to offer, like a lounge area, fire pit, and grill. From $379 per night.

Perks: Outdoor showers, hot tub, fire pit

Checking into this tree-flanked cabin in Wartburg feels like stepping into a luxurious nature retreat. Maybe it’s the pair of waffle robes hung outside the private hot tub deck, or the modern Adirondacks arranged around the fire pit facing the tree line. But that’s just the beginning of the relaxation you’ll experience in your secluded private rental. Here, sliding doors and windows invite you to commune with the great outdoors from every room, while the clean, Scandinavian-style interiors align with the space’s overwhelmingly calming atmosphere. The Solenne is a picture-perfect vacation spot for two, with a king-size floating bed that ensures no one is fighting for space. Consider staying here for a honeymoon, a romantic winter getaway, or a restful solo trip down south. From $219 per night.

Perks: wood barrel stove, sauna, access to 20 acres of land

Nothing says cabin quite like fire pits, fireplaces, saunas, and firewood: all key features of this off-grid cabin. It feels more like a campsite than a standard rental as you won’t have hot water or a refrigerator, but the simpler life does come with at least one special perk: You can sweat your stress away inside the wood barrel sauna. From $283 per night.

Perks: Sauna, fire pit, hot tub, washing machine and dryer

The fittingly named Bird House is a vision of Scandinavian restraint in Cascade, Wisconsin. A path trailing away from the house also leads you to a compact, infrared sauna that fits up to four people. For even more coziness, consider lighting up the fire pit outdoors or stepping into the bubbling hot tub on the back deck. From $305 per night.

Perks: Walk-in shower, outdoor deck, BBQ, fire pit,

Hi-vis SMEG appliances and colorful fiberglass chairs punctuate the white-walled, barebones look of this Scandi-inflected home in upstate New York. In the mornings, sunlight streams in through the skylight overhead to bathe the place in warmth, while at sundown, the surrounding forests in Hunter invite you to tee up the outdoor fire pit and take it all in. From $218 per night.

Perks: full-service kitchen, hot tub, BBQ grill

The term “cozy” is often synonymous with “small.” Not so in this jaw-dropping A-frame that sleeps 10 of your luckiest pals. While the white shiplap interior, floor-to-ceiling windows, and floating staircase create an airy feel, there’s also plenty of texture among the leather, wood and rattan furnishings to warm things up. From $882 per night.

Perks: rainfall shower, wood-burning fireplace

Visitors to this New England town—known to be one of the best ski areas on the East coast—often come to hit the slopes. But even those who have no interest in venturing outside on a cold winter day will relish their visit if they stay at this Scandinavian-inspired cabin. Light wood beams and moldings, thick rugs underfoot, and minimalist furnishings tempt even the most dedicated skiers to stay indoors. While you’re holed up in your new lodgings, enjoy a blissful soak under the rainfall showerhead or take in the view from the glass wall in the bedroom that offers an unobscured view during leaf-peeping season and beyond. From $545 per night.

Perks: outdoor patio, fully-stocked kitchen, luxury linens

An hour outside Boise, situated among the Rocky Mountains, lies a magical escape where you can leave all your stress on the car ride up. This A-frame cabin features luxury amenities, stylish furniture, and views for days (you can choose whether to enjoy them through the floor-to-ceiling windows or while relaxing in the hot tub on the deck).
